He treated the Plastic People's right to make their own music as the same right as the right to publish political dissent.

narratives.title: The Power of the Powerless, 1978
narratives.content: Havel's long 1978 essay The Power of the Powerless described life under late-communist 'post-totalitarianism' as a condition in which citizens were forced to 'live within a lie,' endlessly performing slogans they no longer believed. His famous example was the greengrocer who puts the 'Workers of the World, Unite!' sign in his window not from conviction but from fear. The essay argued that the regime's power depended on this performance, and that it could be broken by individuals refusing to perform it any more.

narratives.title: Four years in prison, Letters to Olga
narratives.content: Havel's longest prison term ran from May 1979 to February 1983. During those years he wrote weekly letters to his wife Olga under strict censorship rules: no politics, no mention of fellow prisoners, no 'humour.' He wrote instead dense philosophical reflections that were later collected as Letters to Olga. The constraint was the form. The letters are a record of a mind that had been given nothing to work with except itself and was determined to work anyway.

narratives.title: Elected president by unanimous vote, December 1989
narratives.content: On 29 December 1989, at the end of the Velvet Revolution, Havel was elected President of Czechoslovakia by unanimous vote of the Federal Assembly. He had been released from his last prison term earlier the same year. He served as the last Czechoslovak president through the 1993 split and then as the first Czech Republic president until 2003. He kept writing plays and essays throughout.

profiles.name: Harriet Tubman
profiles.bio: American abolitionist who escaped slavery in 1849 and returned to the South roughly 13 times between 1851 and 1862 to guide approximately 70 enslaved people to freedom. Scout and spy for the Union Army during the Civil War.
profiles.oneLiner: Went back into the dark thirteen times after she had already gotten out.

narratives.title: The second escape, 1849
narratives.content: In September 1849 Tubman escaped from slavery in Maryland with two of her brothers, but they turned back and forced her to return with them. In October or November of the same year she fled a second time, alone, travelling roughly 90 miles on foot through Delaware to Philadelphia using the Underground Railroad network. She later said that when she crossed into Pennsylvania, 'I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person.' She was not. She was the person who would now go back.

narratives.title: Thirteen missions, approximately seventy people
narratives.content: Between 1851 and 1862, Tubman made roughly 13 documented trips back into slaveholding territory and guided approximately 70 enslaved people to freedom in the Northern states and Canada, while also giving directions to another 50 to 60 who escaped on their own. The logistics involved forged passes, safe houses, code songs, and a personal willingness to use a concealed pistol to stop any rescued person from turning back and endangering the rest of the group. She was nicknamed 'Moses.' There is no record of her ever losing a passenger.

narratives.title: The Combahee Ferry raid, 2 June 1863
narratives.content: During the Civil War, Tubman served the Union Army as a scout and spy in South Carolina. On 2 June 1863 she helped lead the Combahee Ferry raid, guiding Colonel James Montgomery's Second South Carolina Volunteers up the Combahee River to destroy Confederate supplies and liberate the enslaved people working the rice plantations along its banks. More than 700 people were freed in a single day. Tubman became the first woman in US history to lead an armed military operation.

narratives.title: The metal weight and the visions
narratives.content: As a teenager, still enslaved, Tubman was struck in the head by a two-pound iron weight an overseer had thrown at another person. The blow fractured her skull. She lived with severe headaches, seizures and sudden sleep episodes for the rest of her life, symptoms modern scholars have linked to temporal lobe epilepsy or narcolepsy. After the injury she also began experiencing vivid religious visions. She treated them as guidance from God. Her planning of the rescue routes was partly shaped by these episodes.

narratives.title: Auburn, caring for parents and then for the elderly
narratives.content: In 1859 Tubman purchased land in Auburn, New York, and brought her ageing parents to live there. After the Civil War she settled in Auburn permanently, farming the land and eventually founding the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged on property next to her own. In her final years she moved into the Home herself as a resident, paying her own fees out of the meagre pension she had finally been granted as a Union veteran. She died there in 1913.

profiles.name: Frederick Douglass
profiles.bio: American abolitionist, orator, writer and statesman who escaped slavery in 1838 and spent the next 57 years building the most widely read and most widely quoted Black voice in the nineteenth-century United States.
profiles.oneLiner: Taught himself to read and then spent a lifetime making white America listen to what he had read.

narratives.title: Escape, 3 September 1838
narratives.content: On 3 September 1838 Douglass boarded a northbound train of the Philadelphia, Wilmington and Baltimore Railroad at Baltimore, wearing a sailor's uniform supplied by Anna Murray, a free Black woman he was engaged to. He carried forged protection papers borrowed from a free Black sailor. He reached New York City in less than 24 hours. Anna Murray joined him there, and they married 11 days later, on 15 September 1838, the marriage beginning his legal life as a free person.

narratives.title: The 1845 Narrative
narratives.content: Douglass's Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave was published in 1845. He had written it in part because Northern audiences at his speeches had started to disbelieve that a man who spoke so well could actually have been enslaved. The book named his former enslavers, which put him at immediate risk of recapture under the Fugitive Slave Act. He fled to Britain for two years while British supporters raised the money to buy his legal freedom.

narratives.title: What to the Slave is the Fourth of July, 1852
narratives.content: On 5 July 1852 Douglass delivered an address in Corinthian Hall, Rochester, New York, now generally known as 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?' The speech was invited by the Rochester Ladies Anti-Slavery Society as a patriotic address. Douglass used it instead to identify the holiday as a mockery from the standpoint of the enslaved. 'To him, your celebration is a sham,' he said. The speech is now taught as one of the foundational documents of American rhetoric.

narratives.title: Breaking with Garrison on the Constitution
narratives.content: Douglass began his public life as a protege of the radical abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison, who regarded the US Constitution as a 'covenant with death' and wanted disunion. By the early 1850s Douglass had moved to a different reading: that the Constitution, properly interpreted, was actually an anti-slavery document and could be used against the slave system. The shift broke his relationship with Garrison and moved him toward political abolitionism, including eventual support for Lincoln. He treated the break as necessary and unavoidable, not as a betrayal.

narratives.title: Marrying Helen Pitts, 1884
narratives.content: After his first wife Anna Murray died in 1882, Douglass married Helen Pitts in 1884. Pitts was a white suffragist about 20 years his junior. The interracial marriage drew public fury, including from some of Douglass's own children. Elizabeth Cady Stanton sent a congratulatory note. Douglass's recorded answer to the controversy was that his first marriage had honoured his mother's race and the second honoured his father's, and he was done apologising for either.

profiles.name: Jane Addams
profiles.bio: American social reformer and co-founder of Hull House, the Chicago settlement house opened with Ellen Gates Starr in 1889. First American woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, in 1931.
profiles.oneLiner: Moved into the slum on purpose and kept the door unlocked for 46 years.

narratives.title: Opening Hull House, 1889
narratives.content: In 1889 Addams and Ellen Gates Starr moved into a semi-derelict mansion originally built by Charles Hull in 1856 and opened it to the immigrant families of the surrounding Nineteenth Ward of Chicago as a 'settlement house.' Addams funded early repairs personally. The programme grew from a single building into a 13-building complex with a peak of about 2,000 visitors a week. Activities included a night school for adults, a public kitchen, an art gallery, a gym, a music school, a theatre group, a bathhouse and a book bindery. The point was that a single door could lead to any of it.

narratives.title: Sanitary inspector of the Nineteenth Ward
narratives.content: In 1894 Addams was appointed the first woman sanitary inspector of Chicago's Nineteenth Ward. Working with the Hull House Women's Club she reported more than 1,000 health code violations inside a single year, and she treated garbage removal as a literal life-saving intervention. Documented disease and death rates in the ward dropped. She was among the first Americans to make the direct causal link between municipal services and mortality in a poor neighbourhood, using her own data.

narratives.title: The 1915 Hague Congress
narratives.content: Addams chaired the International Congress of Women at The Hague in April 1915, with almost 1,200 participants from both warring and neutral countries meeting in the middle of the First World War. The Congress produced a set of proposals for ending the war by negotiation. Addams and the other leaders then toured European capitals trying to deliver the proposals to heads of state. The mission failed in its immediate goal. It laid the foundation for her eventual Nobel Peace Prize in 1931, which she shared with Nicholas Murray Butler and gave to the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom.

narratives.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House, 1910
narratives.content: Addams's 1910 memoir Twenty Years at Hull-House was written as both a practical account of settlement house work and an argument for a new kind of American civic life. It became a bestseller and is still in print. She used it to make her case that charity from a distance did not work, and that the volunteer had to move in to the neighbourhood she was trying to change. It was autobiographical method as much as content.

profiles.name: Dorothy Day
profiles.bio: American journalist and activist who co-founded the Catholic Worker movement in 1933 with Peter Maurin. Combined radical pacifism, Catholic social teaching and direct hospitality for the homeless for nearly 50 years.
profiles.oneLiner: Sold a newspaper for a penny on Union Square and turned it into houses that fed strangers for the rest of the century.

narratives.title: The Catholic Worker, 1 May 1933
narratives.content: On 1 May 1933, in the depths of the Depression, Day and Peter Maurin brought out the first issue of The Catholic Worker newspaper on Union Square in Manhattan and sold it for one cent. It has been continuously published at one cent per copy ever since. Day wrote much of it herself, by hand, in the margins of the other work she was doing, including running the first of the movement's Houses of Hospitality shortly after.

narratives.title: Conversion after Tamar
narratives.content: In 1925, during her years as a Greenwich Village journalist living with the biologist Forster Batterham, Day became pregnant and on 4 March 1926 gave birth to her daughter Tamar Teresa. Batterham opposed both the pregnancy and organised religion. Day chose, against his wishes, to have Tamar baptised. On 28 December 1927 Day herself received conditional baptism at Our Lady Help of Christians on Staten Island, with a Sister of Charity as her godparent. Her relationship with Batterham ended. The religious turn was a decisive and deliberate break from the bohemian life she had been living.

narratives.title: Houses of Hospitality
narratives.content: From the mid-1930s onward the Catholic Worker movement opened Houses of Hospitality across the United States, offering food and shelter to any homeless person who came to the door, without intake forms, conditions or proselytising. By 1941 there were more than 30 independent Catholic Worker communities. Day insisted on voluntary poverty as a rule for the staff, who lived in the houses alongside the people they were serving rather than going home to separate apartments at night.

narratives.title: Arrested at 75 with the farmworkers, 1973
narratives.content: In June 1973, at age 75, Day joined Cesar Chavez's United Farm Workers picket lines in California and was arrested alongside other supporters, serving ten days in jail. She had also been arrested in 1917 for suffrage picketing and in the mid-1950s for refusing to take part in mandatory civil defence drills in New York City. The consistency across 56 years of arrests, from suffrage to civil defence to farmworkers, is the clearest evidence of her actual politics: whatever was the cause that put poor people against the police, she would be on the picket line.

profiles.name: Studs Terkel
profiles.bio: American oral historian, broadcaster and writer. Hosted The Studs Terkel Program on Chicago's WFMT radio from 1952 to 1997. Author of Hard Times (1970), Working (1974) and The Good War (1985), which won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction.
profiles.oneLiner: Turned the country's anonymous cab drivers, waitresses and steelworkers into the authors of its history.

narratives.title: 45 years on WFMT
narratives.content: From 1952 to 1997 Terkel hosted The Studs Terkel Program on WFMT in Chicago, an hour-long weekday broadcast that ran for 45 years. The guest list over the decades included Martin Luther King Jr., Leonard Bernstein, Bob Dylan, James Baldwin, Buster Keaton, and an almost endless supply of people who had never been on the radio before. The show was essentially unscripted. Terkel treated every guest the same way, famous or not, and the mix itself, a steelworker after a novelist after a concert pianist, was the format.

narratives.title: Hard Times, 1970
narratives.content: Terkel's 1970 oral history Hard Times collected interviews with ordinary Americans who had lived through the Great Depression. He interviewed bankers, dustbowl migrants, unemployed autoworkers, former child labourers and bootleggers, and printed their stories with minimal editorial commentary. The book redefined what an oral history could be, and it reset the genre for the next 40 years. He carried a reel-to-reel tape recorder to most of the interviews and transcribed them personally afterwards.

narratives.title: Working, 1974
narratives.content: His next major book, Working: People Talk About What They Do All Day and How They Feel About What They Do, came out in 1974 and interviewed people at almost every job an American could hold: hotel piano player, telephone operator, grave digger, prostitute, steelworker, doorman, film critic. The book was adapted into a Broadway musical in 1978 and a PBS special in 1982. Terkel's thesis in the introduction is that work is 'about a search for daily meaning as well as daily bread,' and the interviews are his evidence.

narratives.title: Pulitzer for The Good War, 1985
narratives.content: The Good War, Terkel's oral history of the Second World War, was published in 1984 and won the 1985 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction. Terkel had placed the title in ironic quotation marks to push back against the sentimental American memory of the conflict. The book lets former soldiers, nurses, Japanese internment camp detainees and war workers contradict each other at length. The committee gave it the prize anyway.

profiles.name: Jimmy Carter
profiles.bio: 39th President of the United States, 1977 to 1981. Founded the Carter Center in 1982 and spent the following four decades on election monitoring, disease eradication, and Habitat for Humanity house-building. Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002.
profiles.oneLiner: Lost an election and then spent 44 years proving that the post-presidency was the real job.

narratives.title: Founding the Carter Center after losing, 1982
narratives.content: Carter lost his 1980 re-election bid badly to Ronald Reagan. In 1982, a year after leaving the White House, he founded the Carter Center in Atlanta with his wife Rosalynn. The Center was deliberately small and modest in staff, and deliberately specific in mandate: peace negotiations, election monitoring, and the eradication of neglected tropical diseases. It was the opposite of the ceremonial post-presidency that most of his predecessors had chosen.

narratives.title: Guinea worm from 3.5 million to 14
narratives.content: When the Carter Center took on dracunculiasis, or Guinea worm disease, in 1986, there were about 3.5 million annual cases in 20 countries across Africa and Asia. By 2023 the number of reported cases was 14, and the disease remained endemic in only five countries. It is the closest humanity has ever come to eradicating a parasitic disease. Carter followed the programme personally for decades, travelling into affected villages to inspect filtration cloths and water points in his 80s and 90s.

narratives.title: Monitoring 115 elections in 40 countries
narratives.content: Under Carter's direction the Carter Center developed one of the most respected election observation operations in the world. Between 1989 and the early 2020s the Center observed 115 elections in roughly 40 countries. The missions followed a consistent methodology of sending observers in well before voting day and publishing frank post-election reports, including on elections inside the United States. The seriousness of the work derived partly from Carter's own willingness to tell host governments the unwelcome finding in person.

narratives.title: Sunday school in Plains
narratives.content: For decades after leaving the White House, Carter taught Sunday school at Maranatha Baptist Church in Plains, Georgia, most weeks he was home. Tourists from around the country drove through the night to hear the former president teach a Sunday school lesson on, for example, the Book of Ruth. He kept doing it into his 90s. The pattern is the smaller daily twin of the Carter Center's work: the same insistence that the post-presidency was not a ceremonial retirement.

narratives.title: Habitat for Humanity hammers
narratives.content: From 1984 onward, Carter and Rosalynn spent one week each year with Habitat for Humanity's Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter Work Project, personally building homes alongside volunteers at sites in the US and abroad. He was still swinging a hammer on construction sites in his 90s. He died on 29 December 2024 at age 100. The hammer photos from his last decades were used by Habitat as a recruitment tool that proved more effective than any argument about need, because they proved the former president was on the scaffold, and asked why the viewer was not.

profiles.name: Desmond Tutu
profiles.bio: Anglican cleric who became the first Black Archbishop of Cape Town in September 1986 and chaired the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Nobel Peace Prize 1984.
profiles.oneLiner: Turned confession and listening into state-level infrastructure for a country that had no playbook for peace.

narratives.title: The Vorster warning, six weeks before Soweto
narratives.content: In May 1976 Tutu wrote an open letter to Prime Minister B.J. Vorster warning that the maintenance of apartheid would trigger racial violence. Six weeks later the Soweto uprising began, killing at least 660 people over ten months, most of them under the age of 24. The letter did not stop the uprising, but after 1976 it was cited repeatedly as proof that the state had been told plainly, by a clergyman, in plain prose, and had chosen not to listen.

narratives.title: The 1984 Nobel acceptance, addressed to women at railway stations
narratives.content: When Tutu accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 he deliberately diverted the audience away from himself. The speech named, specifically, the mothers who sat waiting at South African railway stations for husbands who had gone off to work in distant mines. 'This award is for mothers, who sit at railway stations... This award is for you.' It is one of the clearest examples in the twentieth century of a public figure using an international podium to redirect attention toward people the world could not see.

narratives.title: Chairing the TRC, 1996
narratives.content: After the 1994 general election Nelson Mandela selected Tutu to chair the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The TRC sat for public hearings from 1996 onwards, with victims and perpetrators in the same room, and Tutu visibly weeping on camera in the opening days. He insisted that the format included testimony from Black and white victims, and that amnesty be conditional on full disclosure. The procedure is now exported as a template for post-conflict societies from Rwanda to Colombia.

narratives.title: August 1980, the Botha meeting
narratives.content: In August 1980 Tutu organised a meeting of twenty church leaders with Prime Minister P.W. Botha and seven government ministers to urge an end to apartheid. The meeting failed. Tutu recorded the failure as a data point, not a humiliation, and kept meeting state officials for another decade. The pattern, quiet persistence in rooms where nothing shifts, became the spine of his method.

profiles.name: Nawal El Saadawi
profiles.bio: Egyptian physician, psychiatrist and writer who published more than fifty books on the condition of Arab women. Founded the Arab Women's Solidarity Association in 1982.
profiles.oneLiner: Wrote her way out of a prison cell with eyebrow pencil on toilet paper, and kept writing until she had built a movement.

narratives.title: The eyebrow pencil and the toilet paper
narratives.content: In September 1981 President Anwar Sadat ordered El Saadawi imprisoned after she helped publish a feminist magazine called Confrontation. In the Qanatir Women's Prison she was denied pen and paper. She used a stubby black eyebrow pencil and a small roll of old and tattered toilet paper to record her thoughts, which later became Memoirs from the Women's Prison. 'I was arrested because I believed Sadat,' she said later. 'He said there is democracy. So I started criticizing his policy and I landed in jail.'

narratives.title: Founding AWSA from inside the prison
narratives.content: While still imprisoned at Qanatir, El Saadawi began drafting the charter for what became the Arab Women's Solidarity Association, the first legal and independent feminist group in Egypt. She founded it formally in 1982, one year after release, describing the organisation as 'historical, socialist, and feminist.' The sequence is worth holding onto. She lost three jobs in one year for the book Women and Sex, then used the enforced silence of prison to design the institution that outlasted every employer who had fired her.

narratives.title: 1972, the price of Women and Sex
narratives.content: Her 1972 book Women and Sex confronted female circumcision and domestic violence in clinical, first-person prose drawn from her practice as a rural doctor in Kafr Tahla. The consequences were specific and immediate: she was dismissed from her post as Director of the Ministry of Public Health, lost her chief editor role at a health journal, and was removed from the Assistant General Secretary role at the Egyptian Medical Association. Three positions, one book, one year.

narratives.title: The rural patient who sent her home
narratives.content: Early in her medical career she tried to protect a rural woman in her home village of Kafr Tahla from her husband's violence. The intervention was read as insubordination by the authorities and she was summoned back to Cairo. The pattern, of moving a specific patient's specific injury into a public argument, is the spine of every book she wrote afterwards.

profiles.name: Toni Morrison
profiles.bio: American novelist, Nobel laureate 1993, and the first Black woman senior editor in the fiction department at Random House, where she worked from the late 1960s until 1983.
profiles.oneLiner: Edited the books that built the Black canon with one hand and wrote the ones that finished it with the other.

narratives.title: 4am with two children asleep upstairs
narratives.content: Morrison wrote her first novel, The Bluest Eye (1970), by getting up every morning at 4am to work while raising two sons on her own and holding a full-time editorial job at Random House. She finished the manuscript and published the book at age 39. The habit of that hour stayed with her. In later interviews she described the pre-dawn window as the only time she could find a sentence that was hers before the world took back her attention.

narratives.title: Acquiring Muhammad Ali and Angela Davis at Random House
narratives.content: As a senior editor at Random House from the late 1960s through 1983, Morrison commissioned and edited Muhammad Ali's autobiography The Greatest: My Own Story (1975), Angela Davis's autobiography, Toni Cade Bambara's fiction, Gayl Jones's fiction, and The Black Book (1974), an anthology of Black American photographs and documents from slavery through the 1920s. The Black Book project is where she found the true story of Margaret Garner, the enslaved woman who killed her own daughter rather than let her be returned. That fragment became Beloved.

narratives.title: Championing Henry Dumas after his death
narratives.content: Morrison used her Random House platform to champion Henry Dumas, a little-known novelist and poet who had been shot to death by a New York City transit officer in 1968. She kept Dumas in print, wrote introductions, and placed his stories in anthologies. The pattern, of editorial care as a form of literary resurrection, became one of her most quiet and consistent practices.

narratives.title: Nobel acceptance, 1993
narratives.content: In her Nobel Prize acceptance lecture in Stockholm in December 1993, Morrison told a parable about an old blind woman and a bird that may or may not be alive in the hands of a visiting child. The speech ended with a sentence that became one of the most quoted lines in her career: 'We die. That may be the meaning of life. But we do language. That may be the measure of our lives.'

profiles.name: James Baldwin
profiles.bio: American novelist and essayist who left New York for Paris in November 1948 with forty dollars and a Rosenwald Fellowship, and built a body of essays that reshaped the American conversation about race, sexuality, and self.
profiles.oneLiner: Translated private humiliation into public argument with the precision of a courtroom stenographer.

narratives.title: November 11, 1948, Paris with forty dollars
narratives.content: Baldwin left New York for Paris on November 11, 1948, at age 24, with forty dollars in his pocket and a 1,500 dollar Rosenwald Fellowship. He later said the move saved his life. Removed from the daily pressure of American racism and the small lies required to navigate it, he finished Go Tell It on the Mountain, which he had been trying to write since he was fourteen. He submitted the manuscript to Knopf in February 1952; the novel was published in May 1953.

narratives.title: Notes of a Native Son, compiled from seven years of essays
narratives.content: Notes of a Native Son, published in 1955, was not a fresh composition. It was a compiled collection of essays Baldwin had placed, one by one, between 1948 and 1955 in Commentary, The New Leader, Partisan Review, The Reporter, and Harper's. The shape of his public voice came out of seven years of quiet magazine work. For many white American readers in 1955 it was the first time they had read a Black writer arguing in the register of a New England essayist.

narratives.title: Cambridge Union, 1965, against Buckley
narratives.content: In February 1965 Baldwin debated William F. Buckley Jr. at the Cambridge Union on the motion that the American Dream had been achieved at the expense of the American Negro. Student spectators voted overwhelmingly for Baldwin. The footage still circulates. The debate is a case study in how to hold a public argument without raising one's voice, and in how to ground an abstract proposition in a single concrete image. Baldwin talked about the cost of cheap cotton.

narratives.title: The 1963 Time cover and the meeting with Kennedy
narratives.content: Baldwin landed on the cover of Time in May 1963 while The Fire Next Time was on the bestseller list. That same month Attorney General Robert Kennedy asked him to gather a group of Black artists and activists to meet privately in New York to discuss race relations. Baldwin brought Lorraine Hansberry, Harry Belafonte, and a young civil rights field worker whose testimony made Kennedy visibly uncomfortable. The meeting ended badly. Baldwin later treated the day as proof that the distance between the Kennedy administration and the movement it claimed to support was not rhetorical, it was factual.

profiles.name: Seamus Heaney
profiles.bio: Irish poet, Nobel laureate 1995, born in County Derry. Refused the Poet Laureate position and declined inclusion in The Penguin Book of Contemporary British Poetry (1982) on the grounds that his passport was green.
profiles.oneLiner: Wrote poems about bog bodies instead of slogans and made the Troubles bearable in print without ever softening them.

narratives.title: Silence-breaking, not rabble-rousing
narratives.content: When Heaney published Requiem for the Croppies, a poem about rebels from the 1798 uprising, readers read it as a veiled IRA anthem. Heaney refused the framing. 'To read it wasn't to say up the IRA or anything,' he said. 'It was silence-breaking rather than rabble-rousing.' That phrase, silence-breaking rather than rabble-rousing, became a kind of private constitution for his relationship to the Troubles. He held it across four decades, three collections of bog poems, and one Nobel prize.

narratives.title: The Penguin letter, 1982
narratives.content: When the editors of The Penguin Book of Contemporary British Poetry (1982) included his work without asking, Heaney published a verse reply titled An Open Letter. The poem contains the line: 'My passport's green. No glass of ours was ever raised / To toast The Queen.' It is one of the few times in twentieth-century poetry a writer used a formal published poem as the vehicle for a polite refusal of a national category. The Penguin editors removed him from subsequent editions.

narratives.title: Beowulf in a Heaney register, 1999
narratives.content: Heaney's 1999 verse translation of Beowulf won the Whitbread Book of the Year. He did not modernise the poem. He imported the rhythms of the speech of older farmers from his father's generation in County Derry into Anglo-Saxon meter, producing a version in which the poem sounded like it had been overheard in a kitchen. The translation sold in numbers that no academic Beowulf had ever reached, and is now the standard text in most American undergraduate courses.

narratives.title: 1972, leaving Belfast for Wicklow
narratives.content: In 1972, with the Troubles intensifying, Heaney left his lectureship at Queen's University Belfast and moved with his family to Glanmore in Wicklow, in the Republic, to write full time. The move was read by some as flight and by others as a vocational commitment. Heaney treated it as the latter. The poems of Field Work (1979) are the direct result of the decision.

profiles.name: Mahmoud Darwish
profiles.bio: Palestinian poet born in al-Birwa in 1941, whose village was razed by Israeli forces during the 1948 Nakba. Joined the PLO in 1973 and wrote the 1988 Palestinian Declaration of Independence.
profiles.oneLiner: Put a stateless nation into lines people could memorise and carry in their pockets.

narratives.title: May 1, 1965, reading Identity Card in Nazareth
narratives.content: On 1 May 1965 Darwish, then 24 and working for the Arab-language newspaper al-Ittihad, read his poem Identity Card aloud at a public gathering in Nazareth. The poem opens with the line 'Write down: I am an Arab.' Within days it had spread across Israel and throughout the Arab world. He was placed under house arrest and later imprisoned multiple times by Israeli authorities specifically for reciting the poem. It is one of the clearest cases in modern literary history of a single poem being treated by a state as a security risk.

narratives.title: Writing the 1988 Declaration of Independence
narratives.content: In 1988 the PLO asked Darwish to draft the text of the Palestinian Declaration of Independence, which Yasser Arafat read in Algiers on 15 November 1988. Darwish wrote it in literary Arabic, with the cadences of classical poetry rather than the flat register of most twentieth-century independence declarations. The document was translated into over thirty languages and is still taught in Arabic schools as a model of literary political prose.

narratives.title: Resigning from the PLO over Oslo, 1993
narratives.content: In 1993 Darwish resigned from the PLO Executive Committee in protest against the Oslo Accords, saying, 'All I saw in the agreement was an Israeli solution to Israeli problems.' The resignation cost him his political position and some of his friends, but freed him to publish poems more critical of the Palestinian leadership than any other senior cultural figure was willing to write at the time.

narratives.title: 1996, a four-day permit to bury a friend
narratives.content: In 1996, more than twenty years after leaving, Darwish was allowed to return to Israel for the first time, on a four-day permit, to attend the funeral of his friend the writer Emile Habibi. He used the visit to walk through what remained of the area around al-Birwa, the village of his birth which had been razed in 1948. He wrote about the visit afterwards in Memory for Forgetfulness, a prose work that treats exile as a repeating act rather than a single event.

profiles.name: Audre Lorde
profiles.bio: American poet and essayist who described herself as 'Black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet.' New York State Poet Laureate 1991 to 1992.
profiles.oneLiner: Refused to separate her identities into manageable portions and made that refusal a public method.

narratives.title: The Cancer Journals, 1980
narratives.content: After a mastectomy for breast cancer in 1978, Lorde refused the prosthesis her surgeon pressed on her and refused to be silent about the refusal. She published The Cancer Journals in 1980 as a mixture of essays and journal entries, arguing that the cosmetic performance of recovery was a form of silencing that served hospitals and magazines more than patients. The book won the American Library Association Gay Caucus Book of the Year Award in 1981 and became one of the first widely circulated first-person accounts of cancer treatment that did not hide the scar.

narratives.title: The Master's Tools speech, NYU 1979
narratives.content: At a feminist conference at NYU in 1979, Lorde delivered a short paper titled The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House, criticising the panel organisers for including only two women of color. The essay, later anthologised in Sister Outsider (1984), contains the line: 'Those of us who stand outside the circle of this society's definition of acceptable women... know that survival is not an academic skill.' It has since been cited in thousands of academic papers. It was delivered, originally, to a room of about two hundred people who had not expected to be addressed.

narratives.title: Founding Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press, 1981
narratives.content: In October 1981 Lorde co-founded Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press with Barbara Smith and Cherrie Moraga. It was the first U.S. publisher dedicated to work by women of color. The press ran out of Smith's Brooklyn apartment for its first years and published This Bridge Called My Back in its second edition, along with work by Lorde, June Jordan, and others. The name was deliberate: the kitchen table is where the decisions got made.

narratives.title: Self-description as practice
narratives.content: Lorde's published self-description, 'Black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet,' is a six-word manifesto. She used it in print, in introductions, on book jackets, and in lectures. The repetition was the point. She was answering, in advance, every interviewer who would later try to list her in a narrower set of identities.

profiles.name: Nina Simone
profiles.bio: American singer, pianist, and civil rights activist born Eunice Waymon in Tryon, North Carolina. Applied to the Curtis Institute of Music in 1950 and was rejected. Received an honorary degree from Curtis two days before her death in 2003.
profiles.oneLiner: Turned a classical conservatory rejection into a protest career that ended with the conservatory apologising on her deathbed.

narratives.title: September 15, 1963, writing Mississippi Goddam
narratives.content: Simone wrote Mississippi Goddam in less than an hour after hearing the news of the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing in Birmingham on 15 September 1963, which killed four Black girls, and with the June 1963 murder of Medgar Evers still fresh. She performed it the next week at a Greenwich Village club. The song was banned in several Southern states and became, in her own account, the piece that ended her commercial career and began her political one.

narratives.title: 1950 Curtis rejection, 2003 Curtis apology
narratives.content: In 1950 Simone, then 17 and still Eunice Waymon, applied to the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia hoping to become the first Black American concert pianist. She was rejected. She believed, until the end of her life, that the rejection was racial, though Curtis denied this. Two days before her death on 21 April 2003 Curtis sent word that she was being awarded an honorary degree. She lived long enough to hear the letter read aloud at her bedside in Carry-le-Rouet, France.

narratives.title: The 1976 Montreux set
narratives.content: Simone's 1976 appearance at the Montreux Jazz Festival, filmed in full, is now one of the most studied live recordings of the twentieth century. She arrived late, berated the audience, forgot lyrics, and then, without warning, pulled the room through a version of Stars by Janis Ian that ended with her weeping at the piano. The film is shown annually in a New York screening and is treated by vocal coaches and performance artists as a primary text on the risks of letting a room in.

narratives.title: September 1970, leaving the country
narratives.content: In September 1970 Simone left the United States after learning of a tax warrant against her for non-payment of taxes she had withheld in protest against the Vietnam War. She went first to Barbados, then to Liberia, then to Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. She did not live in the United States again. The departure was not a pause, it was a full relocation of a career that had been built on American soil.

profiles.name: Mercedes Sosa
profiles.bio: Argentine folk singer, central figure in the nuevo cancionero movement. Arrested on stage during a 1979 concert in La Plata and forced into exile in Paris and Madrid, returning to perform at the Teatro Opera in Buenos Aires in February 1982.
profiles.oneLiner: Gave a continent a set of songs it could sing together when it could not otherwise agree on anything.

narratives.title: 1979, arrested on stage in La Plata
narratives.content: During a 1979 concert in La Plata, Argentina, under the military junta, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage mid-performance, along with every member of the audience. International pressure secured their release. The arrest banned her from performing in Argentina. She relocated to Paris and then Madrid for the next three years. It is one of the few documented cases of an entire audience being detained alongside the performer they had come to hear.

narratives.title: February 1982, return to Teatro Opera
narratives.content: In February 1982 Sosa returned from exile and performed a series of concerts at the Teatro Opera in Buenos Aires. She deliberately invited younger colleagues from the Argentine folk scene onto her stage, treating the return not as a solo victory but as an introduction of a generation. The recordings became the double album Mercedes Sosa en Argentina, which became an instant bestseller and is still the entry point for most listeners outside the Southern Cone.

narratives.title: Gracias a la Vida, 1971
narratives.content: In 1971 Sosa recorded a tribute album to the Chilean folk singer Violeta Parra, who had died by suicide in 1967. The closing track was Gracias a la Vida. Sosa's version, slower and heavier than Parra's original, became the definitive recording and one of the most covered Spanish-language songs of the twentieth century. She performed it at nearly every concert for the next 38 years.

narratives.title: Sistine Chapel and Carnegie Hall in one decade
narratives.content: Sosa performed inside the Sistine Chapel in 1994, and in 2002 sold out Carnegie Hall in New York and the Colosseum in Rome in the same year. She treated the reach as a function of the songs, not of herself. 'An artist isn't political in the party political sense,' she said. 'They have a constituency, which is their public. It is the poetry that matters most of all.'

profiles.name: Fela Kuti
profiles.bio: Nigerian musician who invented Afrobeat in the late 1960s by fusing jazz, funk, highlife, and Yoruba percussion, and used it as a political instrument against successive Nigerian military governments. Founded the Kalakuta Republic commune in 1970.
profiles.oneLiner: Built a song as a political building and dared the army to burn it down, which they did.

narratives.title: 1976 Zombie album and the 1977 raid
narratives.content: Kuti released the album Zombie in 1976. The title track mocked the Nigerian army as unthinking soldiers. In 1977 the government responded by sending around 1,000 soldiers to raid the Kalakuta Republic, his commune in Lagos. The compound was burned. Kuti was severely beaten. His elderly mother, the activist Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a window and died of her injuries. Kuti's response was to deliver her coffin to the gates of the Dodan Barracks military headquarters and to record the song Coffin for Head of State.

narratives.title: 1978, marrying 27 women in a single ceremony
narratives.content: On the first anniversary of the Kalakuta raid, in 1978, Kuti married 27 of the women who lived and worked at the commune in a single ceremony. It was not purely symbolic. He later said the marriages were intended to formalise the relationships so the government could not continue raiding on the pretext of kidnapping. In 1986 he divorced all twelve remaining wives, saying, 'marriage brings jealousy and selfishness.'

narratives.title: Kalakuta Republic as a functioning institution, 1970
narratives.content: Kuti founded Kalakuta Republic in 1970 in the Surulere district of Lagos and declared it formally independent of the Nigerian state. It was not a metaphor. Kalakuta had its own clinic, school, generator, recording studio, and a fence. Musicians from Ginger Baker to Roy Ayers passed through. For seven years it functioned as the home of Africa 70, and a practical demonstration that a musical movement could run itself as a parallel state before the real state destroyed it.

narratives.title: Track lengths that refused radio
narratives.content: Kuti's standard album format ran two tracks, one per vinyl side, each between fifteen and thirty minutes long. The format was chosen deliberately to make the music unplayable on the three-minute commercial radio slots that were the default distribution channel in Nigeria and the UK. The constraint forced the music into live performance, the Shrine venue in Lagos, and album sales, which he could control.

profiles.name: Miriam Makeba
profiles.bio: South African singer known as Mama Africa. Testified before the United Nations Special Committee against Apartheid in 1962 and 1964, after which South Africa revoked her citizenship, leaving her stateless.
profiles.oneLiner: Testified at the UN, lost her country, and sang the next thirty years on nine passports.

narratives.title: July 1962, UN Special Committee on Apartheid
narratives.content: In July 1962 Makeba appeared before the UN Special Committee against Apartheid. She asked the committee to impose an arms embargo on South Africa. The South African government responded by banning her music, revoking her citizenship, and cancelling her right to return, rendering her stateless. She held no South African passport from 1963 until after Mandela's release in 1990. In the interval she was granted nine separate passports by nine different African and European countries so she could travel to perform.

narratives.title: March 1968, losing America by marrying Stokely
narratives.content: In March 1968 Makeba married Stokely Carmichael, the Black Panther and former SNCC chairman. Within weeks her US concerts were cancelled, her US recording contract was not renewed, and, while travelling in the Bahamas, her US visa was refused. She and Carmichael relocated to Guinea. She did not perform in the United States again until 1987. The cost of one marriage, measured in booking sheets, was almost the whole of her American career.

narratives.title: Pata Pata, the song she called insignificant
narratives.content: In 1967 Makeba released Pata Pata, a Xhosa-language song she had first recorded in 1957. It became an international hit and her most commercially successful single. She spent much of the rest of her career mildly annoyed about it. 'Pata Pata is one of my most insignificant songs,' she told interviewers repeatedly. She performed it anyway, because audiences asked for it, and the song paid for the tours that carried her anti-apartheid work.

narratives.title: November 9, 2008, the last concert
narratives.content: On 9 November 2008 Makeba performed at a concert in Castel Volturno, Italy, organised in support of the writer Roberto Saviano, who was under police protection for his reporting on the Camorra. She collapsed after singing Pata Pata and died of a heart attack later that night. She was 76. The choice of concert, held in solidarity with a writer hunted by organised crime, was read by her family as a perfect summary of her method: she went where her presence would protect someone.

profiles.name: Maya Angelou
profiles.bio: American memoirist and poet whose first autobiography, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), was one of the first widely read memoirs by a Black woman in America. Recited On the Pulse of Morning at Bill Clinton's inauguration in 1993.
profiles.oneLiner: Was mute for almost five years as a child and then became the person American presidents asked to speak on their behalf.

narratives.title: Five years of silence after eight
narratives.content: At age eight, Angelou was raped by her mother's boyfriend, Mr. Freeman. She testified at his trial. He was found beaten to death days after his release. Angelou believed her voice had killed him. For nearly five years afterwards she refused to speak. A family friend named Bertha Flowers eventually coaxed her out of silence by telling her, 'You do not love poetry, not until you speak it,' and asking her to read aloud. The entire arc of her later career, six autobiographies and a presidential inaugural poem, is downstream of that single intervention.

narratives.title: January 20, 1993, On the Pulse of Morning
narratives.content: On 20 January 1993 Angelou recited On the Pulse of Morning at Bill Clinton's presidential inauguration. She was the first poet to read at a presidential inauguration since Robert Frost at Kennedy's in 1961, and the first Black poet and first woman ever to do so. The recording won a Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album. Within a week I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings was back on the bestseller list, 24 years after its original publication.

narratives.title: The hotel room, the legal pad, the sherry, the thesaurus
narratives.content: Angelou's writing routine was a fixed ritual. She would check into a hotel room early in the morning, lie down on the bed, and write on yellow legal pads. She kept only a sherry bottle, a deck of solitaire cards, a Roget's Thesaurus, and a Bible in the room. She produced ten to twelve pages a day and edited them to three or four pages by evening, then left by early afternoon. She kept the room booked year-round so she could return whenever a book was active.

narratives.title: Malcolm X in Accra, 1964
narratives.content: Angelou lived in Accra, Ghana from 1962 to 1965 and became close friends with Malcolm X during his 1964 visit. She agreed to return to the United States to help him build the Organization of Afro-American Unity. She was still unpacking her bags in New York when he was assassinated in February 1965. She then worked with Martin Luther King Jr. until his assassination on her 40th birthday in 1968. Both events together moved her from activism into writing. Caged Bird was published the year after King died.

profiles.name: Frida Kahlo
profiles.bio: Mexican painter whose work was almost entirely self-portraiture developed from a hospital bed after a catastrophic bus accident on 17 September 1925. Married to muralist Diego Rivera in 1929.
profiles.oneLiner: Painted her own body from inside it and made self-portraiture carry the political weight of a mural.

narratives.title: September 17, 1925, the streetcar
narratives.content: On 17 September 1925 a Mexico City streetcar collided with the bus Kahlo was riding home from school. She was 18. A steel handrail entered her hip and exited through her pelvis. She fractured her spine in three places, broke her right leg in eleven places, and crushed her right foot. 'The way a sword pierces a bull,' she later wrote. Her medical career, which she had been training for, ended that day. Her painting career began three months later when her mother mounted a mirror above her bed and her father set up an easel so she could work while horizontal.

narratives.title: 1938, the Julien Levy Gallery show
narratives.content: In October 1938 Kahlo had her first solo exhibition at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York. She sold 12 of the 25 paintings on display. It was the first time she had earned money from her own work independent of Rivera's reputation. The following year the Louvre acquired a painting called The Frame, making her the first Mexican artist in their collection. She was 32.

narratives.title: 1953, the stretcher exhibition
narratives.content: In April 1953 Kahlo had her first solo exhibition in Mexico City, at Lola Alvarez Bravo's Galleria de Arte Contemporaneo. Her doctors told her she was too ill to attend. She arrived by ambulance, was carried in on a stretcher, and had her bed installed in the center of the gallery so she could receive guests from it. She died 13 months later. The stretcher opening is now taught as a case study in how an artist can override the staging conventions of their own medium.

narratives.title: The mirror as lifelong studio
narratives.content: Kahlo painted at least 55 self-portraits out of roughly 143 total paintings, a proportion higher than almost any other major twentieth-century painter. She described the reason plainly: 'I paint myself because I am often alone and I am the subject I know best.' The mirror her mother installed above her bed in 1925 remained, functionally, her primary piece of studio equipment for the rest of her life.

profiles.name: Hilma af Klint
profiles.bio: Swedish painter who produced the first fully abstract paintings in Western art around 1906, several years before Kandinsky, Mondrian, or Malevich. Hid the bulk of her work and specified it should not be shown until 20 years after her death.
profiles.oneLiner: Invented abstract art in a side room nobody was watching, then locked the door for 40 years.

narratives.title: The Five, beginning 1896
narratives.content: Starting in 1896, af Klint met weekly in Stockholm with four other women trained at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts. The group, De Fem (The Five), opened each meeting with a prayer, then a meditation, then a Christian sermon, then analysis of a New Testament text, then a séance. In these sessions they produced automatic drawings. Ten years of this practice preceded her abstract breakthrough. The pattern, of treating a weekly small group as a research method, is a clear example of sustained creative infrastructure built outside any institution.

narratives.title: 1906, the Paintings for the Temple commission
narratives.content: In 1906, at age 44, af Klint began the Paintings for the Temple series, which eventually comprised 196 works across multiple sub-series including The Ten Largest, canvases approximately 240 by 320 centimeters depicting the stages of a human life from childhood to old age. She described the commission as having come from an entity she called Amaliel. The first of The Ten Largest predate Kandinsky's first abstract watercolours by around four years.

narratives.title: The 1908 Rudolf Steiner meeting
narratives.content: In 1908 af Klint met the Anthroposophist Rudolf Steiner in Stockholm and showed him the Temple paintings. He was critical. He told her the work was 'inappropriate for a theosophist' and that her contemporaries would not understand it, that it would take another fifty years to decipher. She stopped painting abstract work for four years following the meeting. When she resumed she worked in a more guarded way and began planning the concealment of the work.

narratives.title: The 20-year embargo in her will
narratives.content: Af Klint specified in her will that her abstract work should not be shown publicly until at least 20 years after her death. She left the collection, over 1,200 paintings and 125 notebooks, to her nephew Erik. She died in 1944. The embargo held. When the work finally surfaced in a 1986 exhibition in Los Angeles and then in the Guggenheim's 2018 retrospective, the retrospective drew over 600,000 visitors, the most-visited exhibition in the museum's 60 year history.

profiles.name: Louise Bourgeois
profiles.bio: French-American sculptor whose work was autobiographical across 70 years of practice. Her breakthrough MoMA retrospective came in 1982, at age 70.
profiles.oneLiner: Waited until 70 for her retrospective and then worked for another 28 years at full intensity.

narratives.title: 1982 MoMA retrospective at age 70
narratives.content: Bourgeois's first major retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art in New York opened in 1982. She was 70 and had been making sculpture for over forty years as a peripheral figure. Timed to the show she gave an Artforum interview in which she revealed, for the first time publicly, that her childhood English governess had been her father's mistress and that the imagery in her sculptures, the cages, the figures, the father figures, was wholly autobiographical. A new reading of four decades of work followed the interview.

narratives.title: Maman and the naming of a mother
narratives.content: Bourgeois made the first version of Maman, a steel spider more than 30 feet high, in the late 1990s. It debuted in the inaugural installation of Tate Modern's Turbine Hall in 2000. She explained the dedication directly: 'The Spider is an ode to my mother. She was my best friend. Like a spider, my mother was a weaver.' Her mother had worked in the family tapestry restoration business in France. The sculpture now exists in casts in Bilbao, Ottawa, Tokyo, and Qatar.

narratives.title: The Cells series in her eighties
narratives.content: In her eighties Bourgeois began the Cells series, enclosed installations built from old doors, wire mesh, and found objects. She described them as 'different types of pain; physical, emotional and psychological.' She made more than 60 Cells between 1989 and her death in 2010. The series is evidence that her most sustained and ambitious project arrived in her ninth decade, not her fifth.

narratives.title: The Insomnia Drawings, 1994-1995
narratives.content: Between November 1994 and June 1995, during a period of sleeplessness, Bourgeois made 220 drawings at night in her New York home. She dated each one. The resulting Insomnia Drawings are both an art object and a dated record of 220 nights she could not sleep. She treated the series as a kind of diary her conscious voice could not have written.

profiles.name: Akira Kurosawa
profiles.bio: Japanese film director whose Rashomon (1950) won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 and was the first Japanese film to achieve commercial distribution in the West. Directed 30 films across a career of roughly 50 years.
profiles.oneLiner: Turned every shot into a weather system and every film into a rehearsal for the next one.

narratives.title: August 25, 1950, Rashomon as Western door
narratives.content: Rashomon premiered in Tokyo on 25 August 1950. Daiei, the studio that had produced it, did not understand it. It took a year before the film was entered, over the studio's objections, at the 1951 Venice Film Festival, where it won the Golden Lion on 10 September 1951. The film went on to earn 35,000 dollars in its first three weeks at a single New York theatre, a figure which changed the international distribution economics for Japanese cinema overnight.

narratives.title: Seven Samurai, 148 shooting days, three times the budget
narratives.content: Seven Samurai, released in April 1954, was shot over 148 days spread across nearly a year, and cost three times its original budget, making it the most expensive Japanese film to that date. Kurosawa refused to cut the final battle scene in the rain, which required the studio to wait on weather and then to dump hundreds of tons of water over the set. The rain in the battle is one of the most studied single shots in cinema history.

narratives.title: A Story I Don't Want to Tell
narratives.content: Kurosawa's older brother Heigo, a silent-film narrator, died by suicide in 1933. Kurosawa did not write about it until fifty years later, when he titled the chapter in his autobiography, Something Like an Autobiography, 'A Story I Don't Want to Tell.' The delay is load-bearing. The book otherwise discusses his craft in detail from childhood onwards, and the silence on Heigo is preserved for exactly one chapter, named for its own withholding.

narratives.title: Weather as casting
narratives.content: Kurosawa treated weather as a character to be cast, not a condition to be tolerated. Throne of Blood (1957) was shot in real fog, which he waited for. The battle scenes of Ran (1985) were shot with the sun in exact positions that required the crew to rebuild sets twice. This discipline, of making a schedule subordinate to weather, was extreme even within Japanese studio filmmaking and is now taught as one of his signature craft decisions.

profiles.name: Gabriel García Márquez
profiles.bio: Colombian novelist, Nobel laureate 1982, best known for One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), which sold more than 50 million copies. Began his career as a journalist at El Espectador in 1947.
profiles.oneLiner: Sold his car to buy eighteen months of writing time and came out of it with the defining novel of magical realism.

narratives.title: Selling the car, 1965
narratives.content: Garcia Marquez began writing One Hundred Years of Solitude in 1965 after a revelation while driving to Acapulco with his family. He turned the car around, went home, and locked himself in his study for the next 18 months. To pay for the writing time he sold the car. His wife Mercedes asked for credit from the butcher, the baker, and the landlord, and ran up nine months of unpaid rent. When he finished the manuscript they did not have enough money to post it to the publisher in Buenos Aires in one package, so they sent it in halves.

narratives.title: The 1955 shipwreck series
narratives.content: In 1955, working for El Espectador, Garcia Marquez investigated the case of Luis Alejandro Velasco, a Colombian sailor who had survived ten days on a raft after a naval shipwreck. Over fourteen days Garcia Marquez interviewed Velasco for hours at a time and published the account as a 14-part series. The series contradicted the government's version of events by establishing that the ship had been carrying illegal cargo which had shifted in a storm. The Rojas Pinilla government shut the paper down. Garcia Marquez was sent abroad as a foreign correspondent.

narratives.title: The first sentence, written and rewritten
narratives.content: Garcia Marquez said he rewrote the first sentence of One Hundred Years of Solitude many times before he found the register he wanted: 'Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendia was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.' The sentence contains three tenses and a frame that shifts twice. He said in later interviews that once he had that sentence the remainder of the book came quickly, eight to ten hours a day, for eighteen months.

narratives.title: The Nobel lecture, 1982
narratives.content: In his 1982 Nobel Prize lecture in Stockholm, Garcia Marquez refused to treat magical realism as a formal trick. He argued that the extraordinary history of Latin America, dictators who outlived their own obituaries, plagues that killed whole populations, exiles that lasted lifetimes, was already unrealistic and that European literary categories were the narrow ones. The lecture reframed a decade of critical debate about his work in ten pages.

profiles.name: Georgia O'Keeffe
profiles.bio: American painter who developed a distinctive vocabulary of enlarged flowers, bleached bones, and New Mexico landscapes over a working life of more than 70 years. Married Alfred Stieglitz in 1924 and moved permanently to New Mexico in 1949.
profiles.oneLiner: Painted one flower at the scale of a mural for fifty years and refused to let anyone call it erotic.

narratives.title: Early 1916, charcoal drawings through the mail
narratives.content: In early 1916 O'Keeffe mailed a roll of charcoal drawings to her friend Anita Pollitzer in New York and asked her not to show them to anyone. Pollitzer took them directly to Alfred Stieglitz at his 291 gallery. Stieglitz mounted ten of them in April 1916 without asking O'Keeffe first, calling them 'the purest, finest, sincerest things.' She found out about the exhibition by accident. The confrontation began a correspondence that ended in marriage on 11 December 1924.

narratives.title: Rejecting the sexual reading for fifty years
narratives.content: Almost from the first 1916 exhibition, critics read O'Keeffe's enlarged flowers as sexual imagery. She rejected the reading for the rest of her life. 'When people read erotic symbols into my paintings,' she said, 'they're really talking about their own affairs.' She repeated the correction in essentially identical language in interviews in 1943, 1962, 1977, and 1983. The consistency is striking and is part of the reason the revisionist scholarship of the 1990s onwards began to take the non-sexual readings seriously.

narratives.title: Ghost Ranch, 1934-1949
narratives.content: O'Keeffe first visited Santa Fe and Taos in 1929. She began spending summers at Ghost Ranch, north of Abiquiu, in August 1934. In 1940 she bought property there, in 1945 she bought an abandoned hacienda in Abiquiu, and in 1949, three years after Stieglitz's death, she relocated to New Mexico permanently. The transition from a part of New York's art world to the isolated northern New Mexico high desert took 15 years and was conducted one summer at a time.

narratives.title: Losing her sight, 1972
narratives.content: In 1972, aged 84, O'Keeffe lost most of her central vision to macular degeneration and could no longer paint in oil without assistance. She did not stop working. She began working in clay, then returned to painting with the help of assistants who prepared canvases and described colours for her. She kept working until within a few years of her death in March 1986 at age 98. The fourteen years of work produced after the near-blindness are now part of the late catalogue.

profiles.name: Chinua Achebe
profiles.bio: Nigerian novelist whose first book, Things Fall Apart (1958), has sold over 20 million copies and is the most translated African novel in history. Served as an ambassador for Biafra during the Nigerian Civil War.
profiles.oneLiner: Built an English supple enough to carry Igbo proverbs and then used it to take Joseph Conrad to pieces.

narratives.title: June 17, 1958, Things Fall Apart
narratives.content: Things Fall Apart was published by Heinemann on 17 June 1958, with a title taken from the second line of Yeats's poem The Second Coming. The novel introduced a register of English that could carry Igbo proverbs and ceremonial speech without translation footnotes. It sold slowly at first and then became the first entry in the Heinemann African Writers Series, eventually establishing the publishing infrastructure for a continent's literary canon.

narratives.title: February 18, 1975, the Conrad lecture
narratives.content: On 18 February 1975 Achebe delivered a lecture at the University of Massachusetts Amherst titled 'An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness.' In it he argued that Joseph Conrad was 'a bloody racist' and that Heart of Darkness, a book treated as a classic of moral complexity by Western readers, reduced Africans to props in a white psychological drama. The lecture caused an uproar in English departments and is now one of the founding texts of postcolonial literary criticism.

narratives.title: Biafra, ambassador with a suitcase
narratives.content: During the Biafran War (1967-1970) Achebe served as an unofficial ambassador for the breakaway Republic of Biafra, travelling Europe and North America making the case for recognition. He was travelling when his friend and collaborator, the poet Christopher Okigbo, was killed in action. The Citadel Press, which the two men had co-founded in 1966 to publish African children's literature, never resumed operations. Achebe did not write another novel for 21 years.

narratives.title: The defense of English as the extended frontier
narratives.content: Achebe defended his choice to write in English, rather than Igbo, as a pragmatic one for communication across Nigeria's 500 plus languages and for reaching a post-colonial audience. 'The price a world language must be prepared to pay is submission to many different kinds of use,' he wrote. He argued writers should 'extend the frontiers of English' through mastery, not by ignoring it. The position was controversial in African literary circles, particularly against Ngugi wa Thiong'o, who later renounced English, and the debate is still taught in African literature courses.

profiles.name: Clarice Lispector
profiles.bio: Brazilian novelist born Chaya Pinkhasivna Lispector in Chechelnyk, Podolia (Ukrainian SSR) in December 1920. Her family fled pogroms and arrived in Brazil in 1922. Published Near to the Wild Heart in 1943 at age 23.
profiles.oneLiner: Wrote in a Portuguese that had no precedent and made the language stretch to fit it.

narratives.title: December 1943, Near to the Wild Heart
narratives.content: Lispector was 23 when she published Near to the Wild Heart in December 1943. It won the Graca Aranha Prize in October 1944 and provoked the critic Antonio Candido to write that it was 'the greatest novel a woman has ever written in the Portuguese language.' She had written it in less than a year while working at a news agency in Rio and while her husband Maury Gurgel Valente, a diplomat, was posted abroad. The voice of the novel, interior and non-linear, had no clear precedent in Brazilian fiction.

narratives.title: September 14, 1966, the fire
narratives.content: On 14 September 1966 Lispector fell asleep in bed with a lit cigarette. The fire destroyed her bedroom and nearly cost her her right hand, which she used to write with, and which required multiple surgeries to save. Her legs were permanently scarred. 'I spent three days in hell,' she wrote later. She continued to write afterwards with the damaged hand. The Jornal do Brasil column, which became a major vehicle for her late work, began in August 1967, eleven months after the fire.

narratives.title: 1967-1973, the Jornal do Brasil chronicles
narratives.content: From August 1967 until 1973 Lispector wrote a weekly column for Jornal do Brasil. The chronicles are short, often 500 words, and move between domestic anecdote, philosophical reflection, reader letters, and fragments of fiction. She used the column as a laboratory for the voice that eventually shaped The Hour of the Star (1977). The chronicles are the clearest available record of a serious literary novelist using a newspaper slot as a recurring writing practice across six years.

narratives.title: The Hour of the Star, finished weeks before her death
narratives.content: Lispector finished The Hour of the Star in 1977, the year she died of inoperable ovarian cancer. The novel is narrated by a fictional male writer struggling to tell the story of a poor Brazilian girl from the Northeast. Lispector pasted together drafts on bits of paper during her final illness. The book was published in October 1977. She died on 9 December 1977, the eve of her 57th birthday.

profiles.name: Antoni Gaudí
profiles.bio: Catalan architect who took charge of the Sagrada Familia project in 1883 and devoted his final decade (1915-1926) entirely to its construction. Died on 10 June 1926 after being struck by a tram three days earlier.
profiles.oneLiner: Designed buildings by hanging weights from strings and then built them upside down in his head.

narratives.title: The hanging chain model
narratives.content: To calculate the structural loads of the Colonia Guell crypt and the Sagrada Familia, Gaudi built inverted scale models using weighted strings. He would hang sandbags from chains to map the catenary curves the structure would need to carry, then photograph the model upside down to see the building right-side up. The method bypassed most of the mathematics that contemporary architects used and produced shapes no ruler-and-compass method would have generated. The models still exist in the Sagrada Familia's workshops.

narratives.title: 1915-1926, moving into the site
narratives.content: From 1915 onwards Gaudi devoted himself exclusively to the Sagrada Familia. In his final years he effectively moved into a workshop on the building site and lived there, supervising stonemasons directly. He ceased taking commissions from private clients and subsisted on donations he solicited door to door in Barcelona. The practice, of a celebrated architect literally begging for stonemason wages, is a rare case in the history of the profession.

narratives.title: Trencadis, or mosaics from broken tiles
narratives.content: Gaudi invented the technique now called trencadis, in which broken ceramic fragments from factory waste are assembled into mosaic. He used it across the benches and dragon of Park Guell, the roofs of Casa Batllo, and the Sagrada Familia pinnacles. The practice treats industrial waste as a design medium and predates the contemporary concept of material reuse by roughly a century.

narratives.title: June 7, 1926, the tram
narratives.content: On 7 June 1926 Gaudi was walking to daily mass at the Church of Saint Philip Neri when he was struck by a tram on the Gran Via de les Corts Catalanes. Dressed plainly and carrying no identification, he was mistaken for a vagrant and taken to a pauper's hospital. His identity was only confirmed the following day, when the chaplain of the Sagrada Familia recognised him. He refused to be moved to a better hospital, saying he belonged among the poor. He died on 10 June 1926 at age 73.

profiles.name: Charles and Ray Eames
profiles.bio: American designers whose office in Venice, California (1943-1988) produced furniture, films, exhibitions, and architecture. Designed the Eames Lounge Chair (1956), the Eames House (1949), and the short film Powers of Ten (1968/1977).
profiles.oneLiner: Treated a chair, a house, and a film about the universe as the same design problem.

narratives.title: 1941-1942, plywood leg splints for the Navy
narratives.content: The Eames furniture career started with a Navy contract. In 1941-1942 Charles and Ray developed bent plywood leg splints for wounded soldiers in the Pacific, having figured out how to mould plywood into compound curves in their Los Angeles apartment. The Navy funding allowed them to transition from splints to furniture mass production. The DCW (Dining Chair Wood) and DCM (Dining Chair Metal) chairs, introduced in 1945-1946, are direct descendants of the splint curve.

narratives.title: 1949, Case Study House #8
narratives.content: In 1949 the Eameses completed their own home, Case Study House #8, in Pacific Palisades, California. They assembled it from off-the-shelf industrial steel components ordered from a catalogue. The house is one of the most studied examples in the twentieth century of a building assembled from existing parts rather than custom fabricated. They lived in it for the rest of their working lives. Their studio eventually occupied a former garage at 901 Abbot Kinney Boulevard in Venice from 1943 to 1988.

narratives.title: Powers of Ten, 1968/1977
narratives.content: The Eames Office made Powers of Ten in 1968 and re-released the final version in 1977. The nine-minute film moves the camera in jumps of ten to the power from a picnic in Chicago outward to the edge of the observable universe, then back inward to the quarks inside a hand. It has since been used in high school science curricula worldwide and is now archived by the US Library of Congress. The film is a design object disguised as an educational one. The brief came from IBM.

narratives.title: 1956 Lounge Chair, a gift
narratives.content: The Eames Lounge Chair (670) and Ottoman (671) were designed as a gift for the film director Billy Wilder in 1956. They were intended as a single one-off, a leather and moulded plywood chair with the look of a worn baseball glove. Herman Miller put it into production immediately. It has been in continuous production ever since and is one of the few pieces of twentieth-century designer furniture in the permanent collection of MoMA.

profiles.name: Gertrude Jekyll
profiles.bio: English garden designer and writer who created more than 400 gardens in the UK, Europe, and North America and published 15 books on planting design, including Colour in the Flower Garden (1908).
profiles.oneLiner: Treated a flower bed as a piece of music with a start and an end and taught the whole Arts and Crafts movement to read the score.

narratives.title: The partnership with Lutyens, 1895 onwards
narratives.content: In 1895 the architect Edwin Lutyens, then 25, designed Munstead Wood in Surrey for Jekyll, then 52. It was the first of their house and garden collaborations, which would eventually span dozens of projects including the British Pavilion at the Paris Exposition in 1900 and the Hestercombe gardens in Somerset. Lutyens designed the hard structure. Jekyll designed the planting in its relationship to the hard structure. The partnership is now treated as one of the foundational collaborations of the Arts and Crafts movement.

narratives.title: Colour in the Flower Garden, 1908
narratives.content: In her 1908 book Colour in the Flower Garden Jekyll treated the herbaceous border as a sequence of colour in time. She specified that a 200-foot border should begin in silver-grey and pale blue, move through pink and cream into the hot oranges and reds at the centre, and then return through yellow and pale blue at the far end. She had arrived at the system by studying Turner's paintings and Impressionist colour theory. The book is still in print and is still used by English gardeners as a planning template.

narratives.title: Fifteen books, most written after 56
narratives.content: Jekyll did not publish her first book, Wood and Garden, until 1899, when she was 56. She wrote fifteen books, and most of her 400 plus garden commissions, after the age at which many of her contemporaries retired. Her eyesight was failing throughout the period. She used a magnifying glass to read and wrote in a large, deliberate hand. The late and sustained output is one of the most documented examples of a career's peak arriving well past 60.

narratives.title: Old West Surrey, 1904
narratives.content: In 1904 Jekyll published Old West Surrey, a record of vanishing rural crafts, furniture, and domestic objects in the Surrey villages around Munstead. She spent years photographing and sketching old wheelwrights, ironwork, and cottage interiors before they disappeared. The book is now used by English folk historians as a primary source on late Victorian rural life. It is evidence that her attention to colour and texture was not confined to the garden.

profiles.name: Malcolm X
profiles.bio: American human rights activist who rose through the Nation of Islam in the 1950s, broke from it in March 1964, made the Hajj to Mecca in April 1964, and founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity later that year. Assassinated at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 21 February 1965.
profiles.oneLiner: Rebuilt his worldview in public, on camera, three times in twenty years.

narratives.title: 1948, reading the dictionary in prison
narratives.content: Serving an eight to ten year sentence for larceny at Charlestown State Prison from 1946 onwards, Malcolm Little began a self-education regime that included copying out pages of the dictionary by hand. By his own account he worked through the alphabet letter by letter. The practice was the basis for the later oratorical style: it drew from a larger English vocabulary than the Nation of Islam's speaking tradition used, and it was deliberately constructed inside a prison cell as an instrument for future public argument. He was paroled in August 1952 and began signing his name Malcolm X.

narratives.title: April 1964, the Hajj and the worldview reversal
narratives.content: Within weeks of publicly leaving the Nation of Islam on 8 March 1964, Malcolm X made the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca in April 1964. He wrote letters home from Saudi Arabia describing Muslims of all races eating and praying in the same space and declaring that the racial separation he had preached for twelve years was not supported by Islam as he now saw it. He returned to the United States and publicly repudiated the idea that all white people were the enemy. The reversal cost him support in both the Nation of Islam and parts of the civil rights movement, and he spoke publicly for only ten more months.

narratives.title: The Ballot or the Bullet, April 1964
narratives.content: On 3 April 1964, less than a month after leaving the Nation of Islam, Malcolm X delivered The Ballot or the Bullet in Cleveland, Ohio.
