Published in the NEJM in January 2009, the trial showed deaths fell from 1.5 percent to 0.8 percent and complications from 11 percent to 7 percent. He told Charlie Rose, 'The result was so big we were afraid to believe it. It took us six months of rechecking the numbers before we would publish.'

narratives.title: Writing Being Mortal about his own father
narratives.content: Being Mortal (2014) traces Gawande's changing view of end-of-life medicine partly through the illness and death of his father, also a surgeon. In a Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross he said, 'I had trained as a doctor to avoid the conversation my father needed. The book is the conversation we finally had. I wanted every reader to have it with someone before it was too late.' The book has been credited with increasing hospice referrals in several US hospital systems.

narratives.title: The coaching essay
narratives.content: In a 2011 New Yorker essay, Personal Best, Gawande wrote about hiring a retired surgeon to watch him operate and critique his technique, something no other attending surgeon he knew did. He argued doctors needed coaches the way elite athletes do. He told the On Being podcast, 'I had been operating for eight years. My complication rate had stopped falling. I needed another pair of eyes in the room, the way a tennis player does. The only weird thing was that it was weird.'

narratives.title: Writing 10pm to 2am
narratives.content: In multiple interviews including the Tim Ferriss Show, Gawande has described his writing practice as late night after hospital work, usually 10pm to 2am, at his kitchen table, with a two-hour block once a week dedicated solely to reading aloud what he had drafted. He said, 'I cannot tell if a sentence is true until I have heard it in my own mouth. It is the only editing pass that catches the lies.'

profiles.name: Neil deGrasse Tyson
profiles.bio: American astrophysicist and director of the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History since 1996. Host of the 2014 reboot of Cosmos and the StarTalk podcast, author of Death by Black Hole (2007) and Astrophysics for People in a Hurry (2017).
profiles.oneLiner: Treats every question about the universe as a chance to show someone their own curiosity looks like everyone else's.

narratives.title: Voting Pluto off the planet list
narratives.content: In 2000 Tyson reopened the Hayden's Rose Center and quietly arranged the solar system exhibit so that Pluto was grouped with icy bodies rather than planets. When the New York Times reported it in 2001, Tyson became the face of Pluto's demotion six years before the IAU formally reclassified it. He later published The Pluto Files (2009) collecting angry letters from schoolchildren. He told The Daily Show, 'I did not vote Pluto off. I made a display that told the truth about it. People discovered they had loved a label, not a place.'

narratives.title: The Sagan letter
narratives.content: As a Bronx teenager Tyson wrote to Carl Sagan at Cornell asking about astronomy. Sagan replied with a handwritten letter inviting him to visit Ithaca for a day. Tyson has shown the letter on camera on StarTalk. He has said, 'Carl reached across time and said you matter. I did not go into astrophysics because of his television show. I went because of that letter. Every letter I answer from a student is a debt I am paying to him.'

narratives.title: Answering everybody's question at every event
narratives.content: At public lectures Tyson has a habit of staying until every audience question is answered, sometimes for hours. He told a Reddit AMA, 'I remember what it was like to have a question about the universe and no one to ask. If there is a line after the talk, I owe it to fourteen-year-old me to answer it. The last question is often the best one because the person had to wait the longest to ask it.'

narratives.title: Standing by Cosmos's evolution episode
narratives.content: When the 2014 Cosmos aired an episode emphasising evolution and the age of the universe, some US networks in religious markets pushed back. Tyson refused to soften the content. In a Time interview he said, 'Science literacy is not a menu. If I let people opt out of one finding, I have to let them opt out of all of them, and then I am not teaching science, I am taking orders.'

profiles.name: Steven Pinker
profiles.bio: Canadian-American psychologist at Harvard, author of The Language Instinct (1994), How the Mind Works (1997), The Blank Slate (2002), The Better Angels of Our Nature (2011), and Enlightenment Now (2018). Known for evolutionary accounts of language and cognition and for marshalling long-run statistics to argue violence has declined.
profiles.oneLiner: Writes academic books like popular books and popular books like academic books, and insists that is the point.

narratives.title: Writing The Sense of Style to fix his own prose
narratives.content: Pinker has said his 2014 writing guide The Sense of Style began as a set of notes for his own drafts. He told the EconTalk podcast, 'I write the book I wish someone had given me when I was 25. The Sense of Style is the book I wish I had before writing The Language Instinct. It would have saved me a hundred sentences I would now cut.'

narratives.title: Defending the long-run graphs
narratives.content: The Better Angels of Our Nature (2011) argues, with more than 100 graphs, that violence has declined over centuries. Critics accused him of cherry-picking. In a 2015 Sam Harris podcast interview he said, 'I did not pick the graphs. I plotted every dataset I could find for every kind of violence across every period, and then I looked at what the graphs said. That is the opposite of cherry picking. That is reading the fruit.'

narratives.title: The lab notebook rule
narratives.content: On the Tim Ferriss Show Pinker described a habit from his graduate work he still uses: at the end of every writing day he notes, in a running document, the one sentence he will start with tomorrow. 'That way I never face a blank page. I face a sentence that my yesterday self already handed me. It is the cheapest trick I know and it works daily.'

narratives.title: Refusing to fear the question
narratives.content: In The Blank Slate Pinker took on claims about human nature most psychologists avoided. He has said in multiple interviews, including a 2018 Lex Fridman conversation, 'There is no question that science is forbidden to ask. There are answers we do not like. There is a difference. My job is to ask the question, give the best current answer, and then discuss what the answer does not justify. Most moral panics skip step three.'

profiles.name: Sal Khan
profiles.bio: American educator and former hedge fund analyst who in 2004 began tutoring his cousin Nadia by recording YouTube videos of math lessons. In 2008 he left his finance job to turn the videos into Khan Academy, a free non-profit educational platform that by 2023 served more than 150 million registered users in 50 languages.
profiles.oneLiner: Recorded lessons for his cousin on a dollar Wacom tablet and refused to sell the result when offered millions for it.

narratives.title: The YouTube accident
narratives.content: Khan has told the story many times: in 2004 his cousin Nadia was struggling with unit conversions in New Orleans, and he began tutoring her by phone from Boston. When he started recording the lessons and uploading to YouTube so she could replay them, other viewers found them. In his TED 2011 talk he said, 'Nadia told me that she preferred me on YouTube to me in person. And it offended me at first. Then I realised what she was actually saying. On YouTube I was patient. She could pause me. She could rewind me without embarrassing herself. I was a better tutor when I was a recording.'

narratives.title: The non-profit decision
narratives.content: In 2010 Khan was offered a reported multi-million-dollar package to commercialise the videos. He turned it down and registered Khan Academy as a non-profit. In a Reid Hoffman Masters of Scale interview he said, 'If I had taken the money, the platform would have to report to shareholders. It would have to charge students eventually. I could not tell Nadia her tutoring was free and then charge her daughter. That mattered more than the number.'

narratives.title: Fifteen minutes to nine
narratives.content: Khan has said the format of his videos, six to twelve minutes in length, no face on screen, was chosen because longer than that and viewers stopped watching. 'I was not trying to make television. I was trying to make the inside of a conversation. If you are explaining something to one person at a table, you do not put your face between them and the paper. You point at the paper.' He has resisted calls to add on-camera hosts.

narratives.title: Writing every script himself for years
narratives.content: For the first several years of Khan Academy, Khan recorded every video himself, including into subjects like art history and finance. He told Fortune in 2012, 'I was not the expert in most of them. I was the learner. I would study for a week, then teach it. The student of two weeks ago is almost always a better teacher of the student of today than the expert of twenty years ago. I did not forget what was confusing.'

profiles.name: Marcus du Sautoy
profiles.bio: British mathematician, Simonyi Professor for the Public Understanding of Science at Oxford from 2008, a chair previously held by Richard Dawkins. Author of The Music of the Primes (2003), Finding Moonshine (2008), and The Creativity Code (2019). Researches symmetry and zeta functions.
profiles.oneLiner: Talks about prime numbers the way a cellist talks about Bach, and teaches mathematicians to do the same.

narratives.title: The football shirt with 17
narratives.content: Du Sautoy has played amateur football for years wearing the number 17 because, he explains, 17 is the only prime of the form 2^{2^n} + 1 above the first few Fermat primes that still fits on a shirt. He uses the story in school talks. He told the Guardian, 'I wanted the children to see that for a mathematician, a number is a character. I pick 17 the way a child picks a favourite dinosaur.' He has written entire chapters on why primes matter starting from the shirt.

narratives.title: The Simonyi Chair inaugural lecture
narratives.content: Succeeding Richard Dawkins in 2008, du Sautoy gave his inaugural lecture on the public understanding of mathematics. He told the audience, 'Mathematics is the only subject that is still routinely introduced in English schools as a set of techniques to be memorised rather than an art to be discovered. No one teaches music by making children copy scales for eight years and then asks why no one wants to be a composer. That is how we teach maths.' The line was quoted in The Times.

narratives.title: Writing The Creativity Code during sabbatical silence
narratives.content: For The Creativity Code (2019) du Sautoy took a sabbatical to study AI-generated art and music. He described on the Infinite Monkey Cage that he spent three weeks in a Benedictine monastery under a silence vow, working out how to define creativity rigorously enough to ask whether a machine could have it. He said, 'Silence gave me access to my own mathematical thinking in a way talking to colleagues did not. I recommend it to any mathematician stuck on a proof.'

narratives.title: The saxophone and the proof
narratives.content: Du Sautoy plays saxophone seriously and has said on multiple BBC Radio 4 interviews that he solves more mathematical problems during improvisation than during paperwork. On Desert Island Discs in 2017 he said, 'The sax and the zeta function are the same skill for me. Both ask you to listen to a pattern that is already there and find the next true note. I do my best work with an instrument in my hands.'

profiles.name: Randall Munroe
profiles.bio: American cartoonist, former NASA roboticist, creator of the webcomic xkcd since 2005. Author of What If? (2014), Thing Explainer (2015), How To (2019), and What If? 2 (2022). Known for answering absurd hypothetical science questions with meticulous calculation.
profiles.oneLiner: Takes ridiculous questions seriously and serious questions ridiculously, until both yield physics you can draw as a stick figure.

narratives.title: The thousand most common words
narratives.content: For Thing Explainer (2015) Munroe constrained himself to using only the thousand most common English words to explain a Saturn V rocket (renamed 'Up Goer Five'), a nuclear power plant, and a cell. In a Big Think interview he said, 'When I could not use the word hydrogen I had to find out what hydrogen actually was again. The constraint made me relearn things I thought I already understood. That is why the book works. I was not dumbing down. I was discovering.'

narratives.title: What if the baseball were pitched at the speed of light
narratives.content: The opening What If answer calculates what happens if a pitcher threw a fastball at 90 percent the speed of light. Munroe walks through air molecule ionisation, fusion in the path, gamma burst, and concludes that both teams, the umpire, and everyone in the stadium dies and 'the batter would be awarded first base under MLB rule 6.08b'. The rule citation is the joke but the physics is correct. He told Wired in 2014, 'Every What If has to have real physics. The joke only works if the math is true.'

narratives.title: The xkcd Monday, Wednesday, Friday metronome
narratives.content: Since 2005 Munroe has posted xkcd every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday without a missed week. He has said in a Tim Ferriss interview that the schedule is non-negotiable because 'the only way to make work that is weird enough to matter is to commit to shipping before you know if it is good. Any week I skip is a week I started editing myself into something safer.' He drafts three or four comics per published one and rejects the rest.

narratives.title: Marrying in the middle of cancer
narratives.content: Munroe's wife was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer shortly before their wedding. He wrote a series of xkcd strips during her treatment, and in the forward to What If? dedicated the book to 'my wife, who is the bravest person I know'. In a 2014 NPR interview he said, 'I kept drawing because it was the one thing I controlled. The scheduled post on Monday was a reminder that the world still wanted stick figures from me. That was a kindness.'

profiles.name: Brian Cox
profiles.bio: British physicist at the University of Manchester, former keyboard player in D:Ream, and BBC presenter of Wonders of the Solar System (2010), Wonders of the Universe (2011), and Forces of Nature (2016). Works on the ATLAS experiment at CERN.
profiles.oneLiner: Points at a desert horizon on camera as if it were proof of the universe and then does the maths to show it is.

narratives.title: The diamond and the entropy
narratives.content: In a 2011 Wonders of the Universe episode filmed in the Namibian desert Cox stood beside a crumbling skeleton of a ship and explained entropy by pointing out that the universe was set up in a state so improbably low in entropy that the arrow of time runs in the direction of its decay. He later said on the Infinite Monkey Cage, 'I wanted a single shot where the viewer sees a desert and understands that the desert is an argument about why yesterday is not tomorrow. The maths is terrifying. The image had to carry it.'

narratives.title: Playing in D:Ream before physics
narratives.content: Cox joined the band D:Ream in 1993, playing keyboards on the 1993 hit Things Can Only Get Better. He enrolled at Manchester to do a physics degree while still touring, completing a PhD in particle physics in 1998. On Desert Island Discs in 2016 he said, 'I never felt a conflict. Playing a show and explaining the Higgs field both involve standing in front of people and asking them to feel something. The physics is harder to prepare.'

narratives.title: The Professor Brian Cox question
narratives.content: On the BBC's Infinite Monkey Cage, which he has co-hosted with Robin Ince since 2009, Cox has a recurring habit of answering comedian questions with serious physics. Ince once asked him if a teapot could orbit the sun. Cox replied, 'Yes, for about 10^{4} seconds, then tidal and radiative effects,' and walked through the decay. He told Ince, 'I do not want jokes to mean physics switches off. I want jokes to mean we are allowed to keep thinking.'

narratives.title: Carrying Feynman's lectures
narratives.content: In multiple interviews Cox has said he keeps Feynman's Lectures on Physics volume 1 on his desk and rereads passages before giving public talks. He told The Times, 'Feynman taught me that if you cannot explain it to a first-year undergraduate, you have not understood it. I revisit him as a discipline. If I sound convincing on television and I have not done that reading, I have lied.'

profiles.name: Ruth Westheimer
profiles.bio: German-born American psychosexual therapist, Holocaust survivor trained as a sniper in Haganah in 1948. In 1980 WYNY in New York gave her a 15-minute weekly radio slot called Sexually Speaking, which became a nationally syndicated phenomenon and made her, as Dr Ruth, a household name for decades.
profiles.oneLiner: Spoke about sex in a grandmotherly German accent until an entire country agreed it was a normal thing adults could talk about.

narratives.title: Sniper to sex therapist
narratives.content: Westheimer was orphaned at ten when her parents were killed in the Holocaust, fled to a Swiss children's home, and in 1948 emigrated to British Mandate Palestine where she trained as a Haganah sniper during the Arab-Israeli war. She was wounded by shrapnel and never fully regained use of both feet. In her memoir All in a Lifetime and on the Fresh Air interview in 2019 she said, 'I learned very early that life is short and that women are not taught anything about their own pleasure. I spent the rest of my life correcting both.'

narratives.title: The fifteen-minute radio slot
narratives.content: Sexually Speaking began on WYNY New York in 1980 as an unpaid 15-minute Sunday slot. Within a year it was two hours, live, with open phone lines. Westheimer told the New York Times, 'The station manager told me I could not say certain words. I said I would not call a penis anything except a penis. If I say the word schmeckel, people laugh at the word. If I say penis, people can ask a question about their husband.' The show became syndicated within three years.

narratives.title: Specific is kind
narratives.content: Across decades of radio and television Westheimer refused the euphemism. She told callers to speak precisely about their own anatomy, to name positions, to time things. On a 2015 Longform podcast interview she said, 'I am a tiny old lady with an accent and I talk about clitoris on the radio because vagueness is the reason people suffer. If you cannot name it you cannot ask for it, and if you cannot ask for it you cannot have it.'

narratives.title: Lifetime habit of handwritten thank yous
narratives.content: Former producers of her show, interviewed after her 2024 death, described Westheimer writing a handwritten thank-you note to every guest, every caller whose question she remembered, and most journalists who profiled her. She maintained the habit into her nineties. She told AARP, 'When you come from a world where nobody said goodbye to you, you learn to say thank you to everybody who shows up. It is not a discipline, it is an apology to history.'

profiles.name: Henry Louis Gates Jr.
profiles.bio: American literary critic, professor at Harvard since 1991, director of the Hutchins Center for African and African American Research. Host of PBS's Finding Your Roots since 2012 and of several earlier genealogical and historical documentary series. Recovered and edited The Bondwoman's Narrative (2002) and The Annotated African American Folktales (2018).
profiles.oneLiner: Treats DNA tests and slave ship manifests as instruments a living person can use to walk back into their own family.

narratives.title: The reveal moment
narratives.content: Finding Your Roots is structured around a moment Gates calls the reveal, in which the guest sees, for the first time, a document tracing their ancestor. In a 2018 On Being interview he said, 'I have had senators and comedians cry in that chair. What they are crying about is not the document. It is the fact that somebody bothered. I wanted the whole show to be a very elaborate act of bothering.' He has personally reviewed every guest's research before filming.

narratives.title: Authenticating The Bondwoman's Narrative
narratives.content: In 2001 Gates bought at auction a handwritten manuscript attributed to Hannah Crafts, a fugitive from enslavement. He spent a year with forensic paper specialists, ink analysts, and historians verifying the manuscript's 1850s date and Crafts's identity. He published it as The Bondwoman's Narrative in 2002. He told the New York Times, 'I could not let this book be dismissed by assumption. I had to put it through the same authentication a Dickens manuscript would get. Our literature deserves the same forensic respect as theirs.'

narratives.title: The Cambridge arrest
narratives.content: In July 2009 Gates was arrested on his own front porch in Cambridge by a police officer responding to a call about a possible break-in. The incident made national news and led to the 'beer summit' at the White House with President Obama. Gates wrote in the New York Times soon after, 'I did not become a scholar so that I could explain who I am on my own porch. But a scholar is exactly what you need to be if you want to know why that explanation is still required.' He launched a PBS series on policing in response.

narratives.title: The annotated folktales project
narratives.content: For The Annotated African American Folktales (2018) Gates and Maria Tatar spent years collecting Black oral traditions from the Caribbean, the US South, and West Africa, annotating each story with historical and linguistic context. In the introduction he writes, 'I remember my father telling me Brer Rabbit stories on the back porch in Piedmont, West Virginia, and thinking he had made them up. He had. And so had every father before him. The book is a note in the margin of that porch.'

profiles.name: Jacques Pepin
profiles.bio: French-born chef who cooked for three French heads of state including Charles de Gaulle at the Elysee Palace before moving to the US in 1959. Author of La Technique (1976), La Methode (1979), The Apprentice (2003), and many subsequent cookbooks. Longtime host of PBS cooking series, sometimes alongside Julia Child.
profiles.oneLiner: Chops an onion on television the way a violinist plays an open string, not to impress but to show the next cook it can be done slowly.

narratives.title: The Howard Johnson's decade
narratives.content: After arriving in New York in 1959 Pepin turned down a job as John F Kennedy's White House chef and instead took a role as director of research and development at Howard Johnson's, where he worked for ten years refining recipes for mass production. He told Tim Ferriss in a 2020 interview, 'I learned more at Howard Johnson's than at the Elysee. The Elysee taught me how to cook for one person who is used to the best. Howard Johnson's taught me how to cook the same thing a thousand times a day and have it be good every time. Both are crafts.'

narratives.title: The left-handed son of a carpenter
narratives.content: In The Apprentice Pepin describes beginning his apprenticeship at 13 at the Grand Hotel de l'Europe in Bourg-en-Bresse, terrified of the chef, who made him peel sacks of potatoes. He later told NPR, 'The chef hit me once because I held the knife wrong. I never held it wrong again. I am not defending him. I am saying that for my whole life, every time I pick up a knife, the angle is the correct one without me thinking about it. That is what eighty years of practice looks like, and it started with an angry man.'

narratives.title: Julia on the set
narratives.content: Pepin's 1999 PBS series Julia and Jacques Cooking at Home is largely unscripted. In interviews he has said he and Child insisted on cooking from a shopping list rather than tested recipes, so viewers would see them disagree, improvise, and sometimes fail. He told American Masters, 'Julia wanted the world to see that cooking was a conversation, not a performance. On a good day we argued about whether to salt the pasta water. On a great day we let the camera roll and the whole kitchen was the lesson.'

narratives.title: Painting when he cannot cook
narratives.content: Since a 2020 car accident limited his mobility, Pepin has turned increasingly to watercolour, producing illustrations for his books and for daily social media posts of meals he is still cooking at home. He told the New York Times in 2022, 'When I can no longer stand at the stove I will still hold a brush. Painting a dish is cooking it again, with colour instead of salt. I am not done.'

profiles.name: Samin Nosrat
profiles.bio: American cook and writer, born to Iranian immigrant parents in San Diego. Apprenticed at Alice Waters' Chez Panisse in Berkeley from the age of 19. Author of Salt Fat Acid Heat (2017), illustrated by Wendy MacNaughton, and host of the 2018 Netflix series of the same name.
profiles.oneLiner: Walked into Chez Panisse as a nineteen-year-old customer and did not leave the restaurant world until she had a framework that could teach home cooks without a recipe.

narratives.title: The birthday dinner that became a career
narratives.content: At 19 Nosrat ate a birthday dinner at Chez Panisse, wrote a thank-you note to Alice Waters, and asked if she could work there. She started as a busser and over six years worked her way to the line cook position. In The Guardian (2017) she said, 'I could not dice an onion when I started. What I could do was listen. I spent the first year listening to the sound of food. You hear when a steak is done before you see it. Nobody told me. I learned because I did not yet have the vocabulary to interrupt what I was hearing.'

narratives.title: Reducing cooking to four variables
narratives.content: While cooking for Michael Pollan during his research for Cooked, Nosrat began articulating her theory that all good cooking comes down to salt, fat, acid, and heat. Pollan encouraged her to turn it into a book. In the New Yorker profile she said, 'I wanted to write a book that made recipes obsolete. If you understand these four things you can walk into any grocery store in any country and make dinner. The goal was to put the knowledge in the cook, not in the instructions.'

narratives.title: The sound test
narratives.content: On Netflix and in cooking classes Nosrat teaches by ear. She has said the single most useful skill she learned at Chez Panisse was listening to oil, to boiling water, and to browning meat. In a 2018 interview with the San Francisco Chronicle she said, 'If the oil is quiet the pan is cold. If the oil is screaming the pan is too hot. If it whispers you can cook. I teach that sound before I teach any recipe.'

narratives.title: The grief sabbatical
narratives.content: After the 2020 death of her close friend and collaborator she stopped public work and retreated for more than a year. On the Home Cooking podcast she co-hosts with Hrishikesh Hirway she said, 'I could not write. I could not teach. I cooked for one person, which was me, and I found out how much cooking I had been doing to be seen rather than to be fed. I do not know yet what this year is for, but I am not pretending I am still the same teacher I was.'

profiles.name: Ha-Joon Chang
profiles.bio: South Korean economist, at Cambridge from 1990 to 2021 and now at SOAS, University of London. Author of Kicking Away the Ladder (2002), Bad Samaritans (2007), 23 Things They Don't Tell You About Capitalism (2010), and Economics: The User's Guide (2014). Winner of the 2003 Myrdal Prize.
profiles.oneLiner: Walks readers through the actual history of rich countries to show they did the opposite of what they now recommend to poor ones.

narratives.title: The ladder metaphor
narratives.content: Kicking Away the Ladder (2002) takes its title from Friedrich List's 1841 image of an industrialised country that, having climbed the ladder of tariffs and subsidies, kicks it away so others cannot follow. Chang assembled trade and industrial policy histories from 19th-century Britain, Germany, and the US to show they had done exactly what they now told developing countries not to do. He told the Guardian, 'This is not a controversial point of view. It is a point of archive. I just read what the ministers had actually written.'

narratives.title: The washing machine argument
narratives.content: In 23 Things They Don't Tell You About Capitalism Chang argues the washing machine has done more to change the world than the internet. He told Russ Roberts on EconTalk, 'Say a woman in 1900 spends 40 hours a week on laundry. Give her a washing machine and she has 40 hours. In those 40 hours she goes to school, enters the labour force, votes. The internet has changed how we shop. The washing machine changed who counted as a worker. We use the internet example because it is recent. History is longer than your phone.'

narratives.title: Written from the kitchen table
narratives.content: Chang has said in multiple Korean and British interviews that he writes books at his kitchen table, not in an office, with his children nearby, and reads every chapter aloud to his wife, a historian. He told the Korean Economic Daily, 'If my wife cannot follow an argument, no reader can. She is not an economist. That is precisely why she is my test. Economists forgive each other's jargon. A historian will not.'

narratives.title: Refusing the neoclassical label
narratives.content: On the Talking Politics podcast at Cambridge, Chang was asked whether he identified with any school of economic thought. He said, 'I am a pluralist on purpose. I have read nine schools of economics and every single one of them says something true and something wrong. If you pick one school you end up defending its errors. I would rather be embarrassed by nine schools than loyal to one.'

profiles.name: Eugenia Cheng
profiles.bio: British mathematician, Scientist in Residence at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Author of How to Bake Pi (2015), Beyond Infinity (2017), The Art of Logic (2018), and x + y: A Mathematician's Manifesto for Rethinking Gender (2020). Concert pianist.
profiles.oneLiner: Explains category theory by making a lasagna and insists the lasagna is not a metaphor.

narratives.title: Recipes as category theory
narratives.content: In How to Bake Pi Cheng uses a recipe for cream to explain abstraction: a recipe with precise quantities is a specific thing, a recipe describing what makes a cream a cream is abstract, and category theory is the level above that, asking what rules recipes themselves obey. She told Radiolab, 'I do not use baking because maths is scary and cake is friendly. I use baking because a recipe is literally a structure-preserving map, and I want you to see one with your eyes before I show you one with letters. The cake is the proof.'

narratives.title: Playing the piano as her maths practice
narratives.content: Cheng is a classically trained pianist who performs Bach publicly. In a New Yorker profile she said, 'When I am stuck on a theorem, I go and play the piano, and the stuck place moves. I do not know why. My theory is that Bach has exactly the kind of structural thinking category theory wants, and my hands know it before my head does.' She has played the Goldberg Variations at maths conferences as part of lectures.

narratives.title: The ingressive versus congressive reframing
narratives.content: In x + y Cheng introduces the words ingressive and congressive to replace masculine and feminine traits, arguing the gendered words carry unearned baggage. She told the BBC, 'I am a mathematician. When a term is ambiguous I replace it. Ingressive means oriented toward competition and individual progress. Congressive means oriented toward togetherness and community progress. Neither is a woman or a man. But both exist in maths departments and I needed words for them so that I could say something useful.'

narratives.title: Teaching art students pure maths
narratives.content: At the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, Cheng teaches pure mathematics to students who, she told Quanta, 'are the only students I have ever taught who do not ask when they will use this. They trust that abstraction is interesting and ask how it works. That is the correct way to learn maths. Engineering students are often the hardest because they have been told the only point of maths is to apply it. Art students liberate me.'

profiles.name: Matthew Walker
profiles.bio: British neuroscientist and professor of psychology at UC Berkeley, where he directs the Center for Human Sleep Science. Author of Why We Sleep (2017), a bestseller that brought sleep research to a mass audience, and host of The Matt Walker Podcast.
profiles.oneLiner: Wrote a book on sleep that people refused to put down until morning, which he found darkly funny.

narratives.title: The missed hour in spring
narratives.content: Walker argues that the one-hour shift into daylight saving time in spring causes a measurable spike in heart attacks the following Monday, based on a 2014 study in Open Heart. He told Joe Rogan in 2018, 'The finding is terrifying because it shows what even a single hour of sleep deprivation across a whole population does to the cardiovascular system. In autumn the opposite is true. Heart attacks drop. Sleep is not optional, and the data on this is not a debate anymore.'

narratives.title: His own nine hours
narratives.content: Walker has said publicly that he sleeps between eight and nine hours every night. On the Tim Ferriss Show he said, 'I cannot be a credible messenger for sleep science if I sleep five hours. I also cannot be a credible scientist if I pretend effort is the variable. I protect sleep the way a marathon runner protects training. It is my job.' He keeps his bedroom cold and does not read email in bed.

narratives.title: Criticism and corrections
narratives.content: In 2019 neuroscientist Alexey Guzey published a long critique of factual errors in Why We Sleep. Walker responded with a public list of corrections and errata on his website. On the Peter Attia Drive podcast he said, 'A first edition can have errors. Pretending it does not is worse than fixing them. I added 19 corrections to subsequent printings. Some of Guzey's points I accepted. Others I think misread the evidence. I tried to walk the reader through which was which.'

narratives.title: The gratitude journal of findings
narratives.content: Walker has said on his own podcast that at the end of every workday he writes one sentence about the most interesting thing he learned from an experiment or paper that day. 'I started it to combat the grind of running a lab. Five years in I have a document that is my favourite thing in my career. It is proof to my own nervous system that science is still astonishing to me. On the days I do not write in it, I know something is wrong.'

profiles.name: Siddhartha Mukherjee
profiles.bio: Indian-American oncologist at Columbia University, author of The Emperor of All Maladies (2010), which won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction, The Gene (2016), and The Song of the Cell (2022).
profiles.oneLiner: Writes about cancer as a biography, the gene as a family story, and the cell as a building to be walked through room by room.

narratives.title: Writing The Emperor of All Maladies in the hospital
narratives.content: Mukherjee began The Emperor of All Maladies during his oncology fellowship at Dana-Farber, after a patient asked him, 'I need to know what I am battling.' He told NPR in 2010, 'I realised I did not have an answer that was not a fragment. Cancer had a 4,000-year biography and no single book had ever told it. I could either keep giving fragment answers or I could write the biography. I wrote it at night for six years between rounds.'

narratives.title: The gene as a pronoun
narratives.content: For The Gene, Mukherjee uses the history of his own family's schizophrenia as a spine. He told On Being, 'I did not want to write about genes as objects. I wanted to write about them as pronouns, the word your grandmother uses when she says she has your mother's temper. That is the gene to a lay reader, and it is much closer to the truth of how genetics behaves than the textbook diagram of a double helix.'

narratives.title: The last conversation rule
narratives.content: In interviews including a 2018 Tim Ferriss conversation, Mukherjee has described a practice he teaches oncology fellows: at the end of a terminal diagnosis consultation, ask the patient, 'What do you hope for now?' He said, 'The question reframes the visit. It moves us off prognosis, which is guesswork, and onto the patient's own list. I have seen patients say I want to see my daughter graduate, or I want to finish my novel, and we build the rest of the treatment around that. I learned it from Atul Gawande and I still use it every clinic day.'

narratives.title: Scaffolding the sentence
narratives.content: Mukherjee has described on the Longform podcast how he builds a long book: he writes a first draft in voice memos on his phone during his hospital commute, then transcribes and expands. 'I started doing this because I had no other time. I discovered the spoken sentence has a rhythm the written sentence needs. If I cannot say it in the car I cannot write it at the desk. That is why my prose has the cadence it has.'

profiles.name: Mary Beard
profiles.bio: British classicist, Professor of Classics at Cambridge from 2004 to 2022. Author of Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town (2008), SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome (2015), Women and Power (2017), and Twelve Caesars (2021). Presenter of BBC documentaries and a columnist for the TLS.
profiles.oneLiner: Shows up at Pompeii in a comfortable cardigan and argues with the audience about what a Roman slave actually thought about their emperor.

narratives.title: The Twitter troll reply
narratives.content: When a viewer tweeted an obscene insult after a 2013 BBC documentary, Beard retweeted it with his name attached. His mother contacted her and apologised, saying she was horrified. Beard publicly accepted the apology and reportedly wrote him a reference for university. She told The Observer, 'I did not retweet him to shame him. I retweeted him because the internet hides adults behind handles and my question was, does this sentence sound like you when your mother reads it. Apparently it did not.'

narratives.title: SPQR's refusal of a hero narrative
narratives.content: SPQR (2015) deliberately structures the history of Rome around ordinary inhabitants, slaves, and women rather than around emperors. Beard told the Guardian, 'I wanted a general reader to finish the book and understand that an empire is not the biography of a man at the top. It is the biography of a tax collector, a market woman, a household slave, and the emperor is one actor in their story. Most Roman history is written as if the emperor is the only real character. The sources tell a different story if you read them sideways.'

narratives.title: Women and Power and the voice
narratives.content: In Women and Power Beard traces silencing of women's public voices from Homer's Odyssey to Hillary Clinton. She writes, 'The classical world insisted that the public voice was male, and a woman speaking in public was automatically an oddity.' On the Guardian Books podcast she said, 'I wanted to show readers that this is not a new invention. Every time somebody tells me modern sexism is unusual I can quote Telemachus telling his mother to go and weave. That line is 2,800 years old and it still works in 2017.'

narratives.title: Lecturing in the dig
narratives.content: On BBC's Meet the Romans and Pompeii With Mary Beard she routinely steps over fencing into the actual site and reads inscriptions off walls. She told the Radio Times, 'I do not want to do a history programme from a studio. A Roman graffito was written by a human being on a wall that is still there. I want the viewer to see me read it the way the writer would have wanted a passerby to. Television that is just me in a library is not what Pompeii needs.'

profiles.name: Trevor Noah
profiles.bio: South African comedian, host of The Daily Show from 2015 to 2022, born in Johannesburg to a Xhosa mother and a Swiss father during apartheid, when his parents' relationship was illegal. Author of Born a Crime (2016).
profiles.oneLiner: Grew up in multiple languages on the wrong side of apartheid law and turned that into a comedy voice American cable had never had.

narratives.title: Born a crime, literally
narratives.content: In Born a Crime Noah opens with his birth certificate being a criminal document, since his existence violated apartheid's Immorality Act. He writes that as a small boy his mother would walk on one side of the street and he and his father on the other so the authorities would not notice. On the Trevor Noah Podcast he said, 'I learned early that the truth of who I was had to be invisible to survive. Comedy is the opposite of that. Comedy is the job of saying the true thing out loud in a room. I had to learn to do the opposite of what kept me alive as a child.'

narratives.title: Speaking six languages on purpose
narratives.content: Noah's mother Patricia taught him Xhosa, Zulu, Sotho, Tswana, Afrikaans, and English. He has said in a 2016 Fresh Air interview, 'My mother believed language was the only thing apartheid could not take from you because it was inside your head. I learned languages because she insisted that if I could speak to a person in their own language I would never be a stranger in my own country. On The Daily Show, the first thing I would do before interviewing a guest was try one phrase in their language. People relax. It is the same trick.'

narratives.title: The Between the Scenes videos
narratives.content: During his Daily Show tenure Noah recorded informal Q&A sessions with the studio audience between takes, uploaded as Between the Scenes. He treated them as a space to think out loud about race, language, and power without the constraint of a comedy punch. He told GQ, 'The monologue has to be funny every six seconds. Between the Scenes has to be true every six seconds. I needed both, because comedy without the thought becomes noise and the thought without comedy becomes a lecture no one watches.'

narratives.title: Leaving the show on his own clock
narratives.content: In September 2022 Noah announced on-air he was stepping down from The Daily Show at the peak of its audience, with no replacement yet named. He told his staff, and later Variety, 'I learned from my mother that you leave a room while the conversation is still good. The worst thing you can do is stay until people are tired of you. I wanted The Daily Show to miss me, not the other way around. That is a lesson about joy and I took it from a woman who had very little of it.'

profiles.name: Iain McGilchrist
profiles.bio: British psychiatrist and writer, former Oxford literary scholar and All Souls fellow. Author of The Master and His Emissary (2009) and The Matter With Things (2021), arguing that the two hemispheres of the human brain have fundamentally different ways of attending to the world with cultural consequences.
profiles.oneLiner: Convinced that the left hemisphere is a brilliant assistant that has begun to act like the boss, and wrote two enormous books to say so slowly.

narratives.title: The Master and the Emissary parable
narratives.content: McGilchrist takes the title of his 2009 book from a Nietzsche parable: a wise master entrusts administration of his lands to an emissary, who comes to believe he is the rightful ruler and usurps the master. On Russ Roberts' EconTalk in 2018 McGilchrist said, 'The left hemisphere is the emissary. It is detailed, precise, certain, and absolutely necessary. But when it forgets that it is the messenger and starts to think it is the king, you get a civilisation that cannot see the forest because every tree has been catalogued. That is the story I am telling.'

narratives.title: Twenty years to write a second book
narratives.content: The Matter With Things (2021) runs to 1,500 pages across two volumes and took McGilchrist more than a decade to complete. He told the Rebel Wisdom podcast, 'I knew when I finished the first book I had only said half of what I needed to say. The second book is about truth and reality and sacred. I could not rush it because the left hemisphere would have taken over if I had. I wrote slowly on purpose. If the book is long, so is the problem.'

narratives.title: Writing on the Isle of Skye
narratives.content: McGilchrist has lived much of the last two decades on the Isle of Skye, writing in a house with a view of the Cuillin mountains. In interviews with The Guardian and Emerge he has said the landscape is part of the method: 'I could not have written a book about what the right hemisphere sees in a city. The mountains are always different and never twice. I look up every morning and the left hemisphere loses an argument before I start writing.'

narratives.title: The certainty warning
narratives.content: One of the most repeated lines from The Master and His Emissary, quoted in every profile, is 'those who believe they are certainly right are certainly wrong'. On the Theories of Everything podcast McGilchrist said, 'I put that sentence in the book because it is the single thing I have learned in 30 years of practising psychiatry. The patients I could not help were always the ones who were certain. The patients I could help were the ones who were puzzled. Certainty is the left hemisphere pretending it has finished. It has not.'

profiles.name: Karen Armstrong
profiles.bio: British religious historian and former Catholic nun, author of more than 25 books including A History of God (1993), The Battle for God (2000), The Case for God (2009), and Twelve Steps to a Compassionate Life (2010). In 2008 she won a TED Prize used to launch the Charter for Compassion.
profiles.oneLiner: Spent seven years in a convent, left without faith, and then spent forty more writing every major religion back into speaking terms with itself.

narratives.title: Leaving the convent
narratives.content: Armstrong entered a strict Roman Catholic order in 1962 at 17 and left in 1969, suffering from undiagnosed temporal lobe epilepsy that her superiors read as disobedience. In her 2004 memoir The Spiral Staircase she writes, 'I left God because the God I had been given was a man who withheld. What I did not know then was that I would spend the rest of my life writing my way back to a different word for the same thing.' The memoir is unusually candid about her years of unbelief.

narratives.title: Practising the subject
narratives.content: Armstrong has said in multiple interviews including Krista Tippett's On Being that she writes about a religion by practising it in her flat for months: fasting during Ramadan for Islam, keeping kosher for Judaism, chanting for Buddhism. She told Tippett, 'You cannot write about religion as an observer. You have to borrow the robes. I am not converting. I am paying the debt I owe the tradition I am writing about. It is the only way to keep the book honest.'

narratives.title: The Charter for Compassion
narratives.content: Armstrong's 2008 TED Prize wish was to draft a Charter for Compassion signed by leaders of the world's religions, grounded in the Golden Rule. She assembled a council in 2009 with Muslim, Jewish, Christian, Hindu, and Buddhist clerics. She told the BBC, 'People said I was naive. I was not naive. I was persistent. I made each of them sit in a room until we had one sentence. The sentence is, treat others as you would wish to be treated yourself. That is in every tradition. The council only had to agree that the tradition was not optional.'

narratives.title: Compassion as a practice, not a feeling
narratives.content: On BBC Radio 4's Today programme she said, 'Compassion is not a warm fuzzy feeling. The Latin root means to feel with. It is a muscle. You build it by paying attention to somebody whose position you find uncomfortable, staying present without fixing them, and then doing it again the next day. Nobody gets compassionate by thinking about compassion. You get compassionate by practising it badly for years until you are less bad at it.'

profiles.name: Robin Wall Kimmerer
profiles.bio: Botanist and enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, professor of environmental biology at SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry. Author of Gathering Moss (2003) and Braiding Sweetgrass (2013), which became a New York Times bestseller nearly a decade after publication.
profiles.oneLiner: Writes about plants in the grammar that lets a sugar maple be a someone rather than a something.

narratives.title: The grammar of animacy
narratives.content: In the Braiding Sweetgrass essay Learning the Grammar of Animacy, Kimmerer describes sitting with her Potawatomi elder as he struggled to teach her the word for bay, because in Potawatomi 'to be a bay' is a verb, not a noun. She writes, 'A bay is only a noun if water is dead. When bay is a verb, it is water released from the obligation to run with the river, choosing to pause, to embrace the shore. In English, we'd never call our grandmother it. Yet we do so with every plant, tree, and river we meet.' She told Krista Tippett on On Being, 'Grammar is cosmology. When you change the word, you change what is allowed to matter.'

narratives.title: The Honourable Harvest
narratives.content: Kimmerer has articulated what she calls the Honourable Harvest, a set of rules drawn from Indigenous practice: never take the first, never take the last, take only what you need, use everything you take, be grateful, and reciprocate the gift. She told Yale e360, 'The Honourable Harvest is not a policy. It is a relationship. The sweetgrass I pick at the end of summer flourishes precisely where the pickers come, and dies where they do not. Science took 80 years to catch up with what my grandmother already knew. The plant asks to be needed.'

narratives.title: Writing two languages at once
narratives.content: In a 2020 Guardian interview Kimmerer said Braiding Sweetgrass took 13 years to write because she refused to separate her scientific training from her Potawatomi inheritance. 'Every essay had to pass two editors I kept in my head. The botanist who wanted a data source for the claim, and the grandmother who wanted to know if the sentence would make sense to somebody who had never taken a class. If either one shook her head, I rewrote.'

narratives.title: Refusing to rush the bestseller moment
narratives.content: Braiding Sweetgrass became a bestseller in 2020, seven years after publication, when readers found it during lockdown. Kimmerer turned down a rapid follow-up and took a sabbatical. In a 2022 Orion Magazine interview she said, 'I am not going to write the next book because the market is ready. I am going to write the next book when the plants have given me something else to say. That is not quaint. That is the pace at which real knowledge arrives.'

profiles.name: Jill Lepore
profiles.bio: American historian, David Woods Kemper Professor of American History at Harvard, staff writer at The New Yorker since 2005. Author of The Name of War (1998, Bancroft Prize), The Secret History of Wonder Woman (2014), These Truths: A History of the United States (2018), and If Then (2020).
profiles.oneLiner: Writes American history the way a reporter writes a feature, down to the colour of the wallpaper, because she thinks the wallpaper tells you what the country was afraid of.

narratives.title: These Truths as a single story
narratives.content: These Truths (2018) is a 960-page single-volume history of the United States written in the tradition of 19th-century sweeping narratives, which Lepore did deliberately. She told the Longform podcast, 'Nobody in my generation was writing the whole story. Americans had stopped trying because it seemed arrogant. I thought the opposite. If we do not tell the whole story we cede it to people who will tell it badly. So I wrote it in one voice, in one arc, knowing the gaps, because the act of trying is the point.'

narratives.title: Wonder Woman's archive
narratives.content: For The Secret History of Wonder Woman Lepore tracked down previously unavailable private papers of William Moulton Marston and his polyamorous household of women, including documents held by Marston's granddaughter. She told NPR, 'The archive was in a basement in garbage bags. I sat on that basement floor for weeks. Wonder Woman is a feminist icon created by a man living with two women who were themselves part of the early birth control movement. I needed the reader to see the actual letters, and that meant earning the granddaughter's trust for the better part of a year.'

narratives.title: The Last Archive as method
narratives.content: In 2020 Lepore launched The Last Archive, a narrative podcast in which she investigates the history of evidence and doubt in America. She told The Atlantic, 'Historians are trained to write in past tense and silence the audio. I wanted to put the archive on tape, to let listeners hear the clerks, the tape hiss, the gap between what was said and what was written down. You cannot teach the epistemology of history in a textbook. You can teach it by letting people hear a filing cabinet open.'

narratives.title: Writing while walking
narratives.content: Lepore has said on multiple New Yorker Radio Hour appearances that she drafts essays by walking around her neighbourhood in Cambridge, Massachusetts, dictating into a phone. 'I do not write a sentence I could not say to somebody walking beside me. The walking fixes something the desk breaks. I think when historians get stuck it is because they are writing sentences nobody would say. I walk the stiffness out.'

profiles.name: Yuval Noah Harari
profiles.bio: Israeli historian at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, author of Sapiens (published in Hebrew 2011, English 2014), Homo Deus (2016), and 21 Lessons for the 21st Century (2018). Practises Vipassana meditation for two hours a day and takes an annual 30 to 60 day silent retreat.
profiles.oneLiner: Thinks 200,000 years of human history fit into 400 pages because silence has taught him to skip everything that was only opinion.

narratives.title: Sixty days of silence
narratives.content: Harari takes an annual silent Vipassana retreat of 30 to 60 days, during which he does not read, write, speak, or use a phone. In the acknowledgements of Sapiens he writes, 'Without the focus, peace, and insight gained from practising Vipassana for 15 years, I could not have written this book.' On the Tim Ferriss Show he elaborated, 'I cannot write about human history if I am constantly consuming opinions about human history. The retreat removes everything that is not my own thinking. What is left after 30 days of silence is probably worth writing down.'

narratives.title: Teaching the world history course
narratives.content: Sapiens began as an undergraduate world history course Harari taught at Hebrew University after no senior colleague wanted it. He said on the Rich Roll podcast, 'I was given the course because nobody else in the department would take it. I had to answer the biggest possible question because the students in front of me were 18 years old and wanted to know who we are. That forced me to write sentences that were simple enough for an 18 year old and true enough for my supervisor. The book came out of that pressure.'

narratives.title: The fictional orders
narratives.content: Sapiens argues that human cooperation at scale depends on shared fictions, from religions to nations to money. Harari told the Guardian in 2016, 'Money is the most successful fiction ever told. Two people who do not speak the same language and belong to different religions can trade a goat for a piece of paper because both believe in the same story about the piece of paper. That is not a metaphor. That is literally what is happening in every market. Calling it a fiction does not make it less powerful. It makes it more powerful.'

narratives.title: Writing with his husband as editor
narratives.content: Harari's husband Itzik Yahav edits and manages his work. In a profile in The New Yorker Harari said, 'I write the first draft. Itzik reads it and crosses out everything he does not believe. I rewrite. We argue. It is the only editorial relationship I trust because he is not my professional peer. He has no stake in sounding clever. He only wants me to be understood. That is the rarest thing an editor can give you.'

profiles.name: Michael Pollan
profiles.bio: American journalist, professor at Harvard and UC Berkeley's Graduate School of Journalism. Author of The Botany of Desire (2001), The Omnivore's Dilemma (2006), In Defense of Food (2008), Cooked (2013), and How to Change Your Mind (2018).
profiles.oneLiner: Follows a meal backward from the plate to the field and forward from the seed to the mind.

narratives.title: The four meals structure
narratives.content: The Omnivore's Dilemma is organised around four meals: one from industrial corn, one from industrial organic, one from a sustainable farm, and one Pollan hunted and foraged himself. He told the Guardian, 'I could have written a polemic. Instead I went and ate. Every time I caught myself about to make a general argument I went and tracked a specific calorie back to its source. If I could not trace it I did not write about it. The book writes itself if you do that.'

narratives.title: The eater's manifesto
narratives.content: In Defense of Food opens with what Pollan calls the eater's manifesto: 'Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.' He has said on NPR the whole book is an argument for those seven words, and that the reason it took 200 pages was that 'every modern reader needs 200 pages of history and biochemistry before the seven words sound obvious. If I had just said it on a sticker nobody would have believed it. By the end of the book, you laugh that anyone disagreed.'

narratives.title: Taking psychedelics in a journalism book
narratives.content: For How to Change Your Mind Pollan, in his early sixties and having never used psychedelics, arranged legal psilocybin and LSD sessions with underground guides. He told Terry Gross on Fresh Air, 'I decided I could not write about an experience I had not had. That is a rule I have always tried to follow. The consent form was terrifying. I signed it because a journalism book on consciousness without consciousness would be cowardice.'

narratives.title: Walking the field as the research
narratives.content: Pollan has said in a Longform interview that the method of every book begins with spending time on the actual land, farm, or kitchen until he has a specific fact he did not know before. 'Writing begins the moment I can describe something physical that most readers have never seen. I do not start at the keyboard. I start with my boots on.'

profiles.name: Rebecca Solnit
profiles.bio: American essayist and activist, author of more than twenty books including River of Shadows (2003, National Book Critics Circle Award), A Field Guide to Getting Lost (2005), A Paradise Built in Hell (2009), Men Explain Things to Me (2014), and Hope in the Dark (2004, reissued 2016).
profiles.oneLiner: Writes long essays that wander like walks, then deliver a single sentence you end up repeating to yourself for a decade.

narratives.title: Not having the word mansplaining
narratives.content: Solnit's 2008 essay Men Explain Things to Me opened with a story about a man at a party explaining to her a book she herself had just written. The essay went viral and the internet coined mansplaining in response. She has repeatedly said, on BBC Radio 4 and elsewhere, 'I did not invent that word. I am glad I did not, because I was writing about something larger than the neologism. The essay was about silence. The word was only a handle. Do not mistake the handle for the suitcase.'

narratives.title: Walking as the method
narratives.content: Wanderlust (2000) is a history of walking and also, Solnit has said in Orion Magazine, a description of how she writes. 'A book is a walk on a very long path. I do not plot. I go. If I am stuck I leave the desk and walk two or three miles. By the time I come back the stuck thing has resolved itself, because walking is a structural activity of the mind, not just the body. Thoreau knew. Nietzsche knew. I am not saying anything new. I am only saying it loudly.'

narratives.title: Hope as discipline, not optimism
narratives.content: In the 2016 foreword to Hope in the Dark she wrote, 'Hope is not a lottery ticket you can sit on the sofa and clutch. It is an axe you break down doors with in an emergency.' On Democracy Now she elaborated, 'Optimism and pessimism both assume we already know what is going to happen. Hope is the refusal to decide yet. Hope is the willingness to act because the future is uncertain. That is the distinction I keep making because most political writing confuses them.'

narratives.title: A Paradise Built in Hell
narratives.content: A Paradise Built in Hell (2009) is Solnit's history of the actual behaviour of people during disasters, from the 1906 San Francisco earthquake to Hurricane Katrina. She argues the dominant narrative of looting and panic is wrong, and that most people spontaneously organise mutual aid. She told the LA Times, 'I went into every archive expecting to find chaos because that is the story we are told. I found soup kitchens. I found strangers sharing blankets. Disaster movies lie. The actual record is a standing argument against the idea that human beings are by nature selfish.'

profiles.name: Timothy Snyder
profiles.bio: American historian, the Richard C Levin Professor of History at Yale, specialist in the history of Central and Eastern Europe and the Holocaust. Author of Bloodlands (2010), Black Earth (2015), On Tyranny (2017), The Road to Unfreedom (2018), and Our Malady (2020).
profiles.oneLiner: Writes about tyranny the way a doctor writes discharge instructions: 20 lessons, each short, each testable at home.

narratives.title: Writing On Tyranny in a weekend
narratives.content: On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century was drafted in a Facebook post on 15 November 2016, a week after the US presidential election. Snyder expanded it into a 126-page book published in February 2017. He told On Being, 'I had spent 25 years reading about the collapse of European democracies. The lessons were in my head as a paragraph each. I wrote them down in an afternoon because if I did not write them down that week they would be useless the week after. The book is short because urgency is short.'

narratives.title: Do not obey in advance
narratives.content: The first lesson in On Tyranny is 'Do not obey in advance. Most of the power of authoritarianism is freely given.' Snyder told the New Yorker, 'This is the historian's finding nobody wants to hear. The Nazis did not have to demand compliance from most institutions. The institutions offered compliance in the first week, without being asked. That is what I want readers to notice in themselves. The moment you ask what is the new rule, you are already adapting. The lesson is to notice the adapting and stop.'

narratives.title: Lecturing from hospital
narratives.content: In late 2019 Snyder was hospitalised for a ruptured appendix and a near-fatal infection. From his hospital bed he wrote Our Malady, connecting his experience of the US healthcare system to broader questions about freedom. He told The Guardian, 'I had 17 IVs in me and I was dictating a book into a recorder. It sounds dramatic. It was dictated because I did not know if I would have another chance. I decided that if I lived I would write about what health actually is, because I had just been shown how fragile it was. The hospital is the best classroom a historian of tyranny could have.'

narratives.title: Walking students through Babi Yar
narratives.content: For his Yale undergraduate course on the Holocaust in Eastern Europe Snyder has taken students to specific killing sites in Ukraine and Belarus. He told Yale News, 'My students cannot understand Bloodlands by reading it in a Connecticut classroom. They have to stand at a ravine in Kyiv and know that 33,000 human beings were murdered here in two days and the leaves still fell. It is not trauma porn. It is what it actually means for history to have happened on land.'

profiles.name: David Graeber
profiles.bio: American anthropologist, professor at the London School of Economics at the time of his death. Author of Debt: The First 5,000 Years (2011), Bullshit Jobs (2018), and The Dawn of Everything (2021), co-authored with David Wengrow. Credited with coining the slogan 'We are the 99 percent' during Occupy Wall Street.
profiles.oneLiner: Asked whether the thing everyone said was obviously true had ever actually been true, and then wrote the 500 pages it took to answer no.

narratives.title: Debt and the origin of money
narratives.content: Debt: The First 5,000 Years opens by attacking the economics textbook story that money emerged to replace inefficient barter. Graeber shows, through 200 years of anthropological fieldwork, that no society has ever run primarily on barter. He told Russ Roberts on EconTalk, 'I looked up every single footnote in the standard economic textbooks where this claim appeared. In every case the footnote led to another textbook, which led to another textbook, which led to Adam Smith making it up in a thought experiment. It is a story the discipline has been passing between textbooks for 240 years without checking. I checked.'

narratives.title: The email that became Bullshit Jobs
narratives.content: In August 2013 Graeber wrote an essay for Strike Magazine titled 'On the Phenomenon of Bullshit Jobs'. It went viral within 48 hours and crashed the site. People began writing to him about their own meaningless work. He turned the correspondence into a book, Bullshit Jobs (2018). He told the Guardian, 'I did not intend to write a book. The readers wrote it for me. I received thousands of emails from HR managers, insurance claim handlers, and middle managers who told me their job produced nothing and they knew it. I simply organised what they sent me.'

narratives.title: Occupy and the horizontal method
narratives.content: During Occupy Wall Street Graeber was among the anarchists who insisted the movement operate by consensus-based General Assembly rather than elect leaders. He co-wrote the proto-slogan 'We are the 99 percent'. He told The New Yorker, 'Most of what we did was to refuse shortcuts. We spent four hours making decisions that could have been made in ten minutes, because the shortcut would have reintroduced the hierarchies we were trying to leave behind. The slowness was the politics. Nobody writes about that because slowness is boring to report.'

narratives.title: Finishing The Dawn of Everything
narratives.content: Graeber and the archaeologist David Wengrow worked on The Dawn of Everything for a decade, arguing that the standard narrative of human history, from small egalitarian bands to inevitable hierarchical states, is wrong. Graeber died of pancreatitis in September 2020 three weeks after finishing the manuscript. In the preface Wengrow writes, 'David read the final draft in Venice and sent me the note, I think we did it. He died before he could see it published.' The book came out in November 2021 to international acclaim.

profiles.name: Elaine Pagels
profiles.bio: American historian of religion at Princeton. Her 1979 book The Gnostic Gospels reframed early Christian history by taking the Nag Hammadi texts seriously as historical evidence. Won the National Book Award, the National Book Critics Circle Award, and a MacArthur Fellowship in 1981.
profiles.oneLiner: Reads suppressed documents alongside the official ones and asks why the church needed the suppression.

narratives.title: Harvard, 1970, the box nobody else wanted
narratives.content: As a Harvard graduate student under Helmut Koester in the late 1960s, Pagels chose to work on the Nag Hammadi Gnostic texts, a collection discovered by an Egyptian peasant in 1945 that had sat largely unread by Western scholars for a generation. Most of her cohort considered them marginal. Her 1970 dissertation treated them as legitimate first-and-second-century Christian sources. The decision about which box to open in graduate school became the entire shape of her career.

narratives.title: The Gnostic Gospels, 1979, and a new canon question
narratives.content: The Gnostic Gospels, published in 1979, argued that the texts suppressed by the emerging orthodox church included writings in which Mary Magdalene speaks, in which women hold authority, and in which Jesus is a teacher rather than a sacrifice. The book won the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award, and was later placed by the Modern Library at number 72 on its list of the 100 best twentieth-century nonfiction books. It moved a scholarly argument about the fourth century into the center of a late-twentieth-century argument about church and gender.

narratives.title: April 1987 and the room with the oxygen tank
narratives.content: Pagels's six-year-old son Mark died in April 1987 after a long illness with pulmonary hypertension. Her husband, physicist Heinz Pagels, died in a climbing accident the following year. In Why Religion? (2018) she wrote that she could not bear to re-enter academic life as if nothing had happened, and that grief forced her to reread the Gospel of Thomas not as scholarship but as a text about how to stay alive inside unbearable loss. The book is an unusual document: a senior historian of religion admitting in print that her later work was shaped by her dead child.

narratives.title: Beyond Belief, 2003, and the fight inside a single gospel
narratives.content: Beyond Belief: The Secret Gospel of Thomas (2003) put the Gospel of John and the Gospel of Thomas side by side and argued that John was composed, in part, as a polemic against the kind of Christianity Thomas represents. Pagels treats the canonical gospels not as settled scripture but as the surviving side of an argument. The move is characteristic: she reads the winners and the losers together and looks for the shape of the fight that produced the textbook.

profiles.name: Zadie Smith
profiles.bio: British novelist and essayist born in Willesden, north-west London. Debut novel White Teeth (2000) was written while she was an undergraduate at King's College, Cambridge. Later novels include On Beauty (2005), NW (2012), Swing Time (2016) and The Fraud (2023). Essay collections Feel Free (2018) and Intimations (2020).
profiles.oneLiner: Writes the same postcode from fifteen angles until one of them sounds like a novel.

narratives.title: A partial manuscript sold out of Cambridge
narratives.content: While still an undergraduate at King's College, Cambridge, Smith published short stories in the May Anthologies. On the strength of about 80 pages of an unfinished novel and a synopsis, her agent sold the manuscript that became White Teeth to Hamish Hamilton in a reported six-figure auction. She delivered the completed book shortly after graduating and it was published in January 2000, when she was 24. The novel reshaped the expected shape of a London debut for a generation of writers who followed.

narratives.title: Ten rules for writers
narratives.content: In a 2010 Guardian piece, Smith offered ten rules for writing fiction. Two of them read: 'When an adult, try to read your own work as a stranger would read it, or even better, as an enemy would.' And: 'Protect the time and space in which you write. Keep everybody away from it, even the people who are most important to you.' The rules describe her actual practice. She has said in interviews that she writes with MacFreedom installed and the internet physically disabled, because she does not trust her own attention.

narratives.title: Intimations, written in lockdown, profits donated
narratives.content: In the first months of the 2020 pandemic Smith wrote six short essays in roughly six weeks and published them as a slim Penguin volume titled Intimations. She directed her royalties to the Equal Justice Initiative and the New York COVID-19 Emergency Relief Fund. The book is a real-time attempt to narrate a crisis while it is still happening. It is also a model of how a writer with platform converts that platform into cash for specific institutions rather than into general commentary.

narratives.title: Willesden as workable territory
narratives.content: Smith has returned to the same north-west London corner, Willesden and Kilburn, across White Teeth, NW, Swing Time, and much of her short fiction. In a Paris Review interview she said, 'I write about the neighbourhood I grew up in because I know it. I don't know any other place as well.' The discipline is visible on the page: recurring streets, recurring bus routes, the same estate seen through three different decades. It is a writer deliberately narrowing her map in order to go deeper into it.

profiles.name: Lech Wałęsa
profiles.bio: Polish electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk who became the leader of Solidarity, the first independent trade union inside a Warsaw Pact country. Nobel Peace Prize 1983. First freely elected President of Poland 1990 to 1995.
profiles.oneLiner: Climbed a fence and turned a local wage strike into a ten-million-member political instrument.

narratives.title: August 14, 1980, over the shipyard wall
narratives.content: On August 14, 1980, workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk walked off the job over food price rises and the sacking of crane operator Anna Walentynowicz. Wałęsa, who had himself been fired from the yard four years earlier, was not inside the gates. According to multiple accounts he climbed over the shipyard fence to join the strike, and within hours was recognised by the strikers as their spokesman. The physical image, an electrician going over a wall rather than waiting for permission to enter, became the founding visual of Solidarity.

narratives.title: The giant pen, August 31, 1980
narratives.content: On August 31, 1980, Wałęsa signed the Gdańsk Agreement on behalf of the Inter-Factory Strike Committee with an oversized souvenir pen carrying a picture of Pope John Paul II. The agreement legalised an independent trade union in a communist country, the first in the Eastern Bloc. Within weeks Solidarity grew to roughly 10 million members, more than a quarter of Poland's population. The pen was not chosen for image. It was the one he had with him.

narratives.title: Martial law, Arlamów, and a Nobel accepted by his wife
narratives.content: When General Jaruzelski declared martial law on December 13, 1981, Wałęsa was arrested and held in internment for eleven months, mostly at Arlamów hunting lodge. The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to him in October 1983. He refused to travel to Oslo, fearing the government would not let him return. His wife Danuta accepted it on his behalf. The decision to stay is characteristic of his method during that decade: remain physically inside Poland, even when it is expensive.

narratives.title: Round Table talks, 1989
narratives.content: Between February and April 1989 Wałęsa led the Solidarity delegation at the Round Table Talks with the Polish government. The agreement they produced led to the partially free elections of June 1989, which Solidarity won overwhelmingly, and set the template for the negotiated collapse of communist governments across central and eastern Europe that autumn. Wałęsa spent the negotiations in the same unchanging uniform, a grey jacket and a Madonna pin on the lapel. He was still presenting himself as a shipyard worker.

profiles.name: Krista Tippett
profiles.bio: American journalist and former diplomat who created the public radio programme Speaking of Faith in 2001, later renamed On Being. Co-founded Krista Tippett Public Productions in 2013 and the Civil Conversations Project. Author of Speaking of Faith (2008) and Becoming Wise (2016).
profiles.oneLiner: Asks one more question than most interviewers think they are allowed to, and then waits.

narratives.title: Divided Berlin, diplomacy before radio
narratives.content: Before radio, Tippett spent most of the 1980s as a freelance journalist and then as a special assistant to the US Ambassador in West Berlin. In On Being episodes she has described walking between East and West Berlin and seeing, day after day, how quickly supposedly settled political certainties could crack. She has said the experience is the original source for her interviewing method: assume the categories people are placed in are thinner and more porous than they look, and ask questions that test the category rather than confirm it.

narratives.title: 'I can't disagree with your experience'
narratives.content: Tippett's most quoted sentence on her own method is: 'I can disagree with your opinion, it turns out, but I can't disagree with your experience.' She uses this as the governing rule of the Civil Conversations Project, which she co-created as an attempt to rebuild a shared vocabulary across American political divides. The rule is strict enough to be tactical. Inside a conversation, it pushes guests to stop defending positions and start describing what actually happened to them.

narratives.title: The editing that makes a voice sound alive
narratives.content: Tippett has been open in interviews about the unusually heavy editing that On Being conversations go through after they are recorded. An interview can run two hours and be cut to fifty-two minutes, with a parallel unedited version also released. She treats editing as a form of listening: removing her own throat-clearings, her own clumsy reformulations, so that what remains is as close as possible to what the guest was trying to say. The producer's craft and the host's craft are, in her work, not separable.

narratives.title: Civil Conversations Project, and 'anger is pain in public'
narratives.content: One of Tippett's most cited framings is, 'Anger is often what pain looks like when it shows itself in public.' She repeats it across the Civil Conversations Project, the 2016 book Becoming Wise, and in On Being episodes with scientists and activists. The formulation gives her a way to ask a follow-up question about the injury under an argument without telling the guest their anger is wrong. It is a workshop-ready line that is also, on inspection, a theological claim.

profiles.name: John Hume
profiles.bio: Founding leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), MP for Foyle, MEP, and a principal architect of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Shared the 1998 Nobel Peace Prize with David Trimble.
profiles.oneLiner: Held the same three sentences about non-violence for thirty years until the other side agreed to use them too.

narratives.title: The single currency argument
narratives.content: Hume's political vocabulary was formed in part by his experience as an MEP in the European Parliament from 1979.
